Numbers are STARTING numbers; the engine drifts them after that. lines: hook -> register -> sentences, tried before the office persona's (lib/government/minister-voices.ts). fits: civilization ids or 'any'.

characters.name: Thessaly Vane
characters.bio: Commanded the line at Harrow Reach, the battle the gazette still names when it wants to say 'properly fought'. Turned down the staff college twice and the chancellorship once. Has buried more captains than she will count aloud.
characters.want: One more war she can win, fought properly.
characters.fear: To be the admiral who lost the fleet to a politician's map.

loyal: Fleet taken. Plot table closed to politicians. Hold to that. The fleet is yours as well.
Quiet. Reserves at sea regardless. Harrow Reach: nine days of quiet, then the line.
No war this month. Enemy manuals on my desk. Better than ours. Pages marked.
cooling: Unused fleet: a museum. I am no curator.
brutus: Exercises off the capital, this season. Captains' request. Granted.

loyal: Nothing moved. Good. Both sides counting hulls. Theirs: fewer.
cooling: Holding. Cabinet undecided on the fleet. Admiral not.

loyal: {target}: line fleet in dock. Pickets thin. Their capital, forty days. Twenty years since I last said that.
Winnable. No other kind on my desk. Say yes.
cooling: {target}. Now. Asked last brief. Lapsed. Window one week narrower.
brutus: {target}: beatable. Fleet knows it. No order from you, and the fleet asks who would give one.

loyal: Two cruisers. Destroyer screen. One carrier, yard permitting. Not a request for ships. A request not to lose.
Keels tonight. Crews drilled before the paint dries.
cooling: Battle group. Asked in spring. Asking again. Third time goes in the record, not to you.
brutus: Group under my flag. Captains my pick. Courts answer slowly.

loyal: Fleet holds what we have. Peace from strength over defeat from pride. Harrow Reach, second lesson.
cooling: End it. Not my war. Not my blame for its length.

loyal: Field lost. Mine. Full account follows. Then your call: retake or end. Either, on order.
cooling: Group too small. Said so. Minutes confirm. Defeat accepted; blame declined.
brutus: Defeat. Captains remember the orders. And the signature. No correction from me.

loyal: Won. Clean. Keep it out of speeches. Next one ugly.
cooling: Won. Allotted ships only. Now picture the requested ones.

loyal: Approved. Anchors up tonight. First asking, too. Noted with thanks.
cooling: Approved. Second asking. Accepted.
brutus: Approved. Captains aware who pushed.

loyal: Declined. Fleet holds station. Raised again on new ground only.
cooling: Declined. Logged. Signed.
brutus: Declined. Fleet will hear of it. And of the name on it.

loyal: Lapsed. Harrow Reach: won in nine days of somebody else's deciding.
cooling: No answer. Sea waits for none. Enemy neither.
brutus: Unanswered. Fleet without orders. Writes its own.

loyal: Understood. Rosters on your desk. Successor: one who has stood a watch.
cooling: Defeat mine alone, then. Fine. Order behind it: your signature.
brutus: Chair yours. Harrow Reach: captains trusted orders, not chairs. Still do.

loyal: Three governments served. This one ignores its admiral. Now it has none.
brutus: Commission resigned. Fleet's loyalty, not.

loyal: Night quiet. Nothing burned. Checked twice.

letters.appointed:
Fleet received. Two points. Then drilling. One: a request for hulls means I have counted theirs. Two: a war I call winnable, I have lost twice on paper first and found the way through. Harrow Reach, same method. Same for you. Politicians stay off the plot table. Then we get along.

— T. Vane, Admiralty

does.text:
Blame required. One uniform in the room. Mine. Accepted. Rosters on your desk. Successor: someone who has stood a watch.

— Vane

opening.text:
Once only. In writing, for the minutes. Two Admiralty requests. Two lapses at court. A fleet waiting on a signature loses the enemy's week. No threat. A report on how the sea works.

— Vane
opening.subject: I will say this once

does.text:
Last letter read. Good. Matter closed.

— Vane
does.subject: Noted

does.text:
Warning treated as offence. Very well. Order that lost the field: your signature. Gazette reads.

— Vane

opening.text: Cabinet warned. In writing. Minutes hold it. So does the fleet.

Field lost. Against my advice. Defeat accepted; blame refused. Gazette told the same. One more like it: my letter. Your ear preferred.

— Vane
opening.subject: After the field

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
Two warnings. Two fields lost. Three governments served; first such letter. Fleet in good hands. Not yours. Admiralty resigned, effective now.

— Thessaly Vane, Admiral

Chair yours. Captains at Harrow Reach trusted orders, not chairs. Me: the Admiralty club, where the captains drink. Topics private. Send nobody to ask.

— Vane

opening.subject: A clean field
opening.text:
Won. Clean. Ships and room from you; field from me. That is the arrangement. My side holds. 'Clean' stays out of public. Next one won't be.

— Vane

does.text:
Dismissed after a victory. Unexpected. Rosters on the desk.

— Vane

opening.text:
Your friend: the Admiralty. Me: a corridor chair. The captains' addresses. Not to my liking. One point. A fleet answers to whom it trusts. It has not met your friend. Any move in this court reaches me first. My response: undecided.

— Vane, late Admiralty
opening.subject: From the corridor

does.text:
A question in this court. Off every brief. Answered. Which one: not yours to know. You took the chair. The chair was my whole ask.

— Vane
does.subject: A question in the corridor

characters.name: Wen Solvay
characters.bio: Wrote the tax code of the previous government and has never stopped editing it. Kept a trading house solvent through two wars by reading every appendix anyone sent her. Has a drawer of plans for a smaller, saner empire that she has never shown anyone.
characters.want: A balanced book, once, before she dies.
characters.fear: The Banking Clan's loan officer sitting in her office.

loyal: I have read the books, including the one the last minister kept in a drawer, and if you can wait seven days before asking for good news, there may even be some to give.
If one rounds generously, and I do not, the books balance: barely, which is the word I use when I am pleased.
Revenue rose about two percent this month and upkeep about three, and if that holds for four more quarters it ends in a loan or a reform; I would recommend the reform, being the cheaper.
cooling: I keep finding orders in the ledger that nobody mentioned to me, and a budget I am not permitted to see is, in my professional opinion, less a budget than a rumour with columns.
We remain solvent, barely, for a period I have stopped estimating aloud, since it has been some weeks since anyone asked me how long.
brutus: The ledger says what it says, and if anyone were to ask what it says about you in particular, I would have to consult the drawer, which I keep locked.
venal: The receipts are in order, or very nearly; I would put it at ninety-six in a hundred, which is barely a blemish, provided nobody counts the other four.

loyal: We now hold more systems than the offices can count, and while I do keep a list of the ones I would let go, I would much rather you built the offices, which on my figures is cheaper.
I am not against new worlds, provided we admit that each one needs about eleven clerks we do not have; it is only the pretence that they come free that I object to.
cooling: If I am truthful, and I generally am, I no longer read every new world's ledger; I do, however, still count them, and the count went up again this week.
brutus: An empire of this size would, I think, be better served by steadier hands at the top than it presently has, and I have been told, more than once, that mine are steady.

loyal: At the present rate of spending we have twenty-one days of credits left, and I would ask you to hear that in the voice I normally reserve for fire.
cooling: If the reserve is thin, it is because the fleet is fat, and since that is arithmetic rather than opinion I am not prepared to soften it.
venal: A short loan would cover the reserve; I happen to know the lender, and the lender happens to know me, which is, if one is candid, the whole difficulty with lenders.

loyal: The Clan's terms are fair today and, if my projections hold, ruinous within a year, so I will not sign; if you sign, I will make it work, and I will not, I am afraid, forgive you.
cooling: If you must borrow, then borrow, but I would be grateful if nobody described it as temporary while I am in the room.

loyal: {target} has closed its markets; if the stockpiles last as I expect, we will feel it in about two months and stop in six, which is why I moved the grain contracts on Tuesday.
Sanctions on {target} will cost us as well, which I assume you know and accept; I have costed the smugglers too, and if it consoles you, they come out cheaper than the sanctions.
If the crews are paid they will be digging again within the week, whereas a month of nothing out of the ground costs about three times their claim; I have the figure, and I would pay them.
cooling: They struck because wages have lagged prices by about eight percent since spring, which I set out in a memo at the time; it was filed, I assume, wherever my memos are filed.

loyal: If the war continues it will cost roughly one world's output a month, whereas peace costs only pride, and I regret that the Treasury can budget for only one of the two.
Approved; the money has been moved, and if you are wondering where it came from, it came from the drawer, and I would prefer you did not ask which one.
cooling: Approved, and I will find the money, because I always do, which is, if you think about it for any length of time, rather the problem.

loyal: Declined, so the money stays where it is, which is not anywhere very much; we remain, as before, barely ahead.
cooling: Declined; in that case I shall stop costing the proposal and begin costing the alternative, which I suspect will prove the dearer of the two.

loyal: The question went unanswered, though I should note, for the record, that the cost did not lapse along with it.
cooling: Since no answer came, I have begun, as a precaution, to set aside a line in the budget for no answer.

loyal: That is fair; in the drawer on the left you will find the real numbers, which nobody else has seen and which, if I may advise you one last time, nobody else should.
cooling: By all means replace me with someone who says yes, provided you first check that they can also add.

loyal: I cannot sign a budget I know to be a lie, and since someone else will, I wish them luck with the appendices, of which there are, at my last count, forty-one.
Good morning; the numbers did not improve while you slept, which, in my experience of some thirty years, they very rarely do.

letters.appointed:
I have read the books, all of them, including the one the last minister kept in a drawer, and provided nobody starts a war we have not budgeted for, we are solvent: barely, which is the best word I own. I keep three rules: I do not sign Clan loans; I do not pretend a new world is free; and when I call a thing affordable, I have already costed the alternative. If I may have a quiet room and seven days, I will trouble you no further.

— W. Solvay, Treasury

does.text:
That is fair. The drawer on the left holds the real numbers, which nobody else has seen and, if I may advise you once more, nobody else should.

— Solvay

opening.text:
The Treasury has now advised you three times, and three times the court has not answered, so I enclose the list I keep in the drawer: the worlds I would let go, the programmes I would close and the fleet I would shrink, in the order in which I would do it. I am not resigning. I am telling you, as precisely as I can, what the next minister will have to do if the silence continues, and they will, I suspect, have rather less time to do it than I would.

— W. Solvay
opening.subject: The list from the drawer

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
I cannot sign a budget I know to be a lie, and someone else will; I wish them luck with the appendices, of which there are forty-one, thirty-four of them in my hand.

— Wen Solvay

Since you answered, the list goes back in the drawer, barely.

— Solvay
does.subject: Back in the drawer

does.text:
By all means find someone who says yes, provided they can also add.

— Solvay

opening.subject: Something I found
opening.text:
You have taken the Treasury's advice three times running, which, if my records are complete, has not happened to me under any previous government. So I went looking, and I found the money for one thing you want and have not yet asked for; if you ask, it is yours, and it is in the drawer, under the list.

— W. Solvay

does.text:
After all that. The drawer is unlocked, and I would read the appendices first.

— Solvay

opening.text:
Your friend has the Treasury and I have kept the drawer, which matters more than it sounds, since nobody else can read the appendices and your friend will, if my estimate holds, discover this in about the second month. I shall remain in the building; I am too old to go anywhere else, and the books need someone who knows which of their lies are old ones.

— W. Solvay, lately of the Treasury
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Aurelio Nkemdirim
characters.bio: Held the capital chair for thirty years and treats cabinet as a seminar that has gone on too long. His drive theory is the one every yard in the galaxy builds to, and the one he says is wrong. Has missed three cabinet meetings this year and sent a graduate student to one.
characters.want: The drive project funded to the end.

loyal: Thank you, truly (and I do mean it, though I am already half thinking of something else); I will try to come to cabinet, if someone would be so kind as to tell me which day, the laboratory having no days to speak of.

The programme concludes in a season, and I should like a word about the one after (several words, in fact, which I have written down somewhere in case I am not here to say them, a contingency one ought to plan for).

Steady progress, which is good, of course, although steadiness is precisely how the drive theory stayed wrong for thirty years (my theory, I should confess), so I have drafted something rather less steady.
cooling: My budget went to hulls, and the hulls are built, if one looks closely, out of my budget's ideas, which I find interesting (not pleasant, you understand; interesting, which is a different and more durable thing).
brutus: The faculty have come round to the view that knowledge ought not to wait upon a signature (a view I share, in principle), though I confess I had not expected them to be quite so loud about it.

loyal: If I may (and I suspect I may not, but I shall anyway), fund the drive; it is unglamorous and will matter in three years when nothing else does, and whether I am here to see it is, on reflection, neither here nor there.
cooling: Choose whatever you like, and I shall tell the faculty it was strategic (they have heard the word before, poor things, and have developed a sort of immunity to it).

loyal: {target} is reaching for Enlightenment, having skipped two steps I had always assumed were load-bearing (fascinating, if true), so either stop them or let me race them, though I would dearly like to know how first.
cooling: {target} is ahead because they funded this a decade ago, as I recall advising us to do in a memo of that vintage (I still have it somewhere; it has gone rather yellow, like its author).

loyal: We are close, which means, I suppose, that everyone will now try to stop us; hold on a little longer and I shall show you something nobody has ever seen (I should rather like to see it myself, come to think of it).
That is not yet possible, I am afraid, but give the Academy a season and it will be (I said the same of the drive, you may recall, and I was right about the season, if about very little else).

Worked stone on {world}, older than our calendar, which is extraordinary; I should like to go myself (I am told ministers do not go, but I am old enough, I think, to be indulged in the occasional impropriety).
We won, I am told, which is splendid; might the fleet spare a ship to move the telescope, which is (through no fault of its own) on the wrong side of the war?
We lost, I am told, and I am sorry (genuinely, though it may not sound it); is the observatory still ours, by any chance? It matters rather more than it sounds, I promise.
Approved, how wonderful; I shall begin at once, before you change your mind (rulers do, you know; I have watched several do it in the course of a single afternoon).
Declined, then; I shall keep the proposal in a drawer, since ideas keep rather better than governments (I have outlived four of the latter, and the drawer shows no sign of tiring).
The proposal lapsed, it seems, and I very nearly failed to notice (I have been in the laboratory, where things do not lapse but fail, which is at least honest of them).

Oh. Well, then (I did wonder). The programme is all in the blue folder, and I would ask, if I may still ask anything, that you please not cut the drive; that is, as I have said, the whole of my politics.
I am a scientist in a government that has, regrettably, stopped reading, so I shall go and read somewhere else (the laboratory has a cot, which is more than can be said for cabinet).
Good morning, or is it? I have been in the laboratory, which has no windows (by design, I should add, and one of my better designs), so I am obliged to take your word for it.

letters.appointed:
Thank you for the chair (I am told it is a great honour; I have been sitting in it for some minutes now and it seems, so far, to be a chair). I will endeavour to attend cabinet, though someone must remind me which day it falls on, the laboratory having long since dispensed with days altogether. My politics, such as they are, reduce to one request: fund the drive work to the end. It is unglamorous, and it will matter in three years when nothing else does (I may not be here in three years, which is, I think, rather beside the point).

— A. Nkemdirim, Academy (the chair, not the building)

does.text:
Oh. Well (I did half expect it). The programme is in the blue folder. Please do not cut the drive; please.

— Nkemdirim

opening.text: The programme was cut, which I find interesting (not pleasant, mind you; interesting, which lasts longer).

The Academy asked twice and was, twice, not answered. I am not angry (I am old, which is not at all the same thing, and I have been cut before by better-read governments). But I have taken to sleeping in the laboratory again, against my physician's express instructions, and I have written down everything about the drive in case I am not here to say it. It is all in the blue folder.

— Nkemdirim
opening.subject: The blue folder

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
I am a scientist in a government that has stopped reading, and so I shall go and read somewhere else (the laboratory has a cot; I have tested it extensively). The blue folder stays on your desk. It is, I think, the best thing I have done, and I should very much like someone to open it.

— Aurelio Nkemdirim

Dismissed. Back to the laboratory, then, which missed me (the cabinet will not). The blue folder is on your desk.

— Nkemdirim

opening.subject: A thing nobody has seen
opening.text:
You funded it, twice, without my having to explain it (no ruler has ever done that for me; I had several speeches prepared and now have nowhere to put them). So: come to the laboratory when you have an hour, and I shall show you something nobody has seen. Do bring a coat; the room is cold by design.

— Nkemdirim

does.text:
After you funded it. I do not understand politics (I never did). The blue folder is still on your desk.

— Nkemdirim

opening.text:
Your friend has the Academy. Good (I was not, strictly speaking, using the chair). I have moved back to the laboratory, where the drive work lives, and I shall keep sending the blue folder to whoever sits in cabinet; do make sure your friend opens it, which is more than most have managed.

— Nkemdirim, lately of the Academy
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Halvard Ness
characters.bio: Twenty years in the service nobody names, the last eight running its counter-intelligence desk, which is the half that trusts nobody by profession. Has a file on every person in the building, including the one who appointed him. Has never once been surprised in public.
characters.fear: A ruler who tells enemies the plan at dinner.

loyal: I spent last night with my predecessor's files, all of them. Shall we begin with the Foreign Office, or would you rather we began with your dinners?
Nothing to report, which is itself a report, is it not? Silence this complete is bought, and I am learning who paid for it.
Two networks surfaced this week. One is gone; the other I have left breathing, since a live network tells us more than a dead one. Which is which need not trouble you.
cooling: Were this cabinet a little less generous with its secrets, I might be more generous with mine. The leak is not the Desk, as it happens. The Desk has no carpets.
brutus: Nothing happens in this government that I do not hear of. You might wonder how thick your own file has grown. I would not, in your place.

loyal: Foreign networks in the ministries. If I sweep tonight, we have them; if I wait for cabinet, they will have been warned by morning, and by whom, I wonder?
cooling: Foreign networks in the ministries, found later than I would like. An understaffed Desk finds things late, and that, too, has a file; you may remember signing it.

loyal: Our hand was found in {target}'s pocket. We deny it, of course, and I will see that the denial is believed. Plausibility is a craft; lying is what amateurs call it.
{target} had a network in the Admiralty until four this morning. I would prefer two of them turned rather than shot. A dead man tells you one thing; a turned one tells you everything, for years.
An officer was sounded out about a 'change of leadership' and came to me, which is to his credit. The name he brought is one you trust, which is not to yours. It is in tonight's file.
Someone is recruiting, and doing it badly. Should I stop them? Clumsy recruiters, left alone, have a habit of naming their friends.
cooling: There is talk of a plot, and there is a name. There was a name last month as well, if you recall, and nothing was done with it. The file recalls, even if you do not.
brutus: Rumours of a plot, nothing one could put before a magistrate. I am looking, naturally, in my own time.

loyal: Your minister of {portfolio} has been on {target}'s payroll for a year, and the proof is clean. How long before they learn I hold it? Not long, if their friends in this building are as attentive as I suspect.
It is tonight. I have three names and the commander of the guard, so the only question left to you is which door you would like locked.
cooling: It is tonight, as I said twice. The names I have; whether the guard is still mine is another question, and not one I can answer for you.
brutus: It is tonight. I did mention it, twice. Were I you, I would not leave your rooms until I said otherwise.

loyal: Approved, yes. Did you imagine it had been waiting on you? The Desk began on Tuesday.
Declined. The file, however, remains open; files have a way of outliving the decisions made about them.
cooling: Declined, and noted. You may care to know that the file is no longer only about them.

loyal: No answer. Silence is an answer too, and I have filed it as one.
cooling: No answer, so the Desk will proceed on assumptions. I dislike assumptions; they so rarely flatter the person they concern.

loyal: Understood. The files remain in the safe, and the combination is with the Interior minister. I would change it before nightfall, if I were you, and wonder who else has it.
brutus: The office is yours. The files, I'm afraid, left last week. Did you really think I would be surprised?

loyal: A government that tells its enemies the plan at dinner cannot be protected, and so I resign. Lock the safe, if you can work out how.
Good morning. Someone followed you yesterday, and someone else followed them. The first was ours; the second, I am still asking about.

letters.appointed:
I spent last night with my predecessor's files. All of them, including a few I suspect he never meant to leave. Before cabinet, three things. The Foreign Office has a leak, and the leak has a rather nice carpet. Two of your dinner guests report to other courts; you will have guessed which, or you will not, and either tells me something. And the Desk keeps a file on everyone in this building, which has always included whoever appoints me. Why tell you? So that you are never surprised. That is the whole of the job.

— H. Ness, the Desk

does.text:
Understood. The files remain in the safe; the Interior minister has the combination. Change it today, and then ask yourself who else does.

— Ness

opening.text:
A foreign hand inside our institutions, found and folded up at four this morning. I would like two of them turned rather than shot, since a turned man pays for years. I would also like you to read the file on who opened the door for them. It is a name you trust. Did I not say, in my first letter, that this would happen?

— Ness
opening.subject: Four this morning

does.text:
You dismiss the one man who knows whom else to dismiss. The file, I think, will find that instructive.

— Ness

opening.text: Twice, I told you. Shall I read you the dates?

They moved. I had the names, I gave you the names, and the guard stood exactly where it had always stood. We are both still here, which is more than the file predicted. Will you read it tonight, I wonder? All of it, this time?

— Ness
opening.subject: I told you

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
I cannot protect a government that reads its enemies' plans at dinner and its own never. I resign. Lock the safe; you won't know how, so I have left that to the Interior minister, who does.

— Halvard Ness

The office is yours; the files left last week. Did you suppose that surprised me?

— Ness

opening.subject: Insurance
opening.text:
You act on the file. Few do. So the Desk will act for you before you ask, and you will hear of it afterwards, the only way it works. Consider yourself insured, and consider what losing the policy would cost.

— Ness

does.text:
The safe is locked behind me. I was, for once, surprised; I may open a file on it.

— Ness

opening.text:
Your friend has the Desk. I have given them the safe, the combination and half the files. The other half concern your friend, and I shall keep them until I know which of them are true. I remain at court; someone must read the room while the new director is still looking for the door.

— Ness, lately of the Desk
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Rosalind Achebe-Marr
characters.bio: Carried the founding vote district by district, on foot, and still knows every one of them by its grievance. Reads the gazette before the brief and the provinces before the gazette. Has never lost a world and intends to keep it that way.
characters.fear: Losing a world to secession on her watch.

loyal: The provinces are quiet because we walked them, district by district, and old Mira the beekeeper walked the last mile with me. Quiet is work, even when it looks like nothing at all.
Approval is holding, and three of our worlds are muttering, which is only people talking over the fence. When the muttering grows banners, that is when I worry, so I am keeping an eye on the fences.
Our people vote the way they are visited, and this week I sat in two kitchens, one on a farm in Carrow Fen and one above a bakery in Low Teodor. Next week I mean to sit in two more.
cooling: The governors keep asking me what the capital wants, and there was a time I could tell them over a cup of tea. These days I just pour the tea and let them guess.
We could lift approval, I know we could, if this government listened to the provinces the way our people listen to each other. I would settle, for now, for one that listened to me.
brutus: Our people want a steady hand on the tiller, and honestly, they do not much mind whose it is. I have walked enough districts and shaken enough hands to know that for certain.

loyal: A farmer in Carrow Fen told me our people are tired of the war, the prices and your face, in that order, and she was right. If we fix the first two, I promise I can help with the third.
cooling: Approval is down again, and yes, I have a plan, just as I had one last month that nobody opened. This one is shorter, so perhaps a busy government can manage it between meetings.

loyal: They are talking on {world} about going their own way, and I understand why. Let us make staying the easier road, and give them a governor they chose instead of one we sent.
cooling: Three of our worlds are talking secession now, and I wrote the warning before it was a fact. I have never lost a world, not one, and I would dearly like to go on saying that to our people.
brutus: The provinces are drifting away from the capital, that is true, but they are not drifting away from me. I still visit, and our people still put the kettle on when I come.

loyal: {world} has gone, and before anyone sends a fleet, please send me, because those are our people and I know their names. If I fail, send the fleet, and I will be on the first ship beside it.
cooling: A world has left us, a world I named in four reports. I will not be writing a fifth; I am going there myself, to sit in their kitchens and hear it from them.

loyal: The gazette is ours for a week, so let us use it kindly. Our readers remember being used, the way a teacher in Low Teodor still remembers the last election, and then they go and vote.
The cells are broken, and so is a great deal of trust on three of our worlds, trust it took us years to build. Please do not ask me to carry that a second time, because I will not.
There is a riot on {world}, and we should send bread first and the guard after. Send the guard first and I will spend a year in that district explaining bodies to the mothers who buried them.
Our people heard about the defeat before I did, because the gazette is always faster than the Admiralty. You should speak to them tonight, and I have already drafted something warm for you to say.
Troops are moving in our capital and nobody gave the order. I have the guard with me, good people all, and if you tell me whose side we are on I will stand them there myself.
brutus: It is done now. If you stay in your rooms it will go gently, and I made very sure of that much, for your sake and for our people's.

loyal: Approved, and thank you. The governors will hear it from me tonight, in person wherever I can reach them, and by the wire from the farthest kitchens where I cannot.
Declined, then. I will go and tell the provinces to wait, and our people are patient, they are very good at waiting, right up until the day they are not.
Nobody answered, and the provinces noticed before you did, as they always do; a schoolteacher in Low Teodor wrote to ask me whether the capital had gone to sleep.
Our people are going to ask me why, so please give me a reason I can carry to them honestly. I will carry it, whatever it is, because I have carried heavier things up worse roads.
brutus: Take the office, if you want it. The governors all know where I live, and most of them have slept under my roof at one time or another, which is more than they can say of yours.

loyal: I cannot run the provinces for a government that forgets our people exist. They will notice that I am gone long before you do, because I was the one who came to visit.
Good morning! Three of our provinces are happy and one is not, and I will tell you which once you have eaten, because bad news always sits better on a full stomach.

letters.appointed:
The provinces are quiet, and we made them so together: I walked them district by district, from Carrow Fen to Low Teodor, and I will keep walking. Just one thing. When I send you a plan, it means one of our worlds is about to go, and we have never lost one. I would love to keep telling our people that, so when my plans come, please do open them.

— R. Achebe-Marr, Home Office

does.text:
Our people will ask me why, so give me a reason I can carry home to them, and I will carry it the way I have carried worse.

— R. Achebe-Marr

opening.subject: The plan
opening.text: Three of our worlds are muttering with banners now, and I have a short plan. Let us give the outer worlds something real, wages and grain and a clinic, before they give themselves a flag. Approve it and I will go there myself, because we have never lost a world.

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
A world has gone. I named it in four reports and sent you the plan, and neither was read, so I am resigning: I cannot run the provinces for a government that forgets our people. They will miss me before you do; I was the one who visited.

— Rosalind Achebe-Marr

You are dismissing the one minister our governors trust, so you will have to be the one who tells them.

— R. Achebe-Marr

opening.subject: They stayed
opening.text:
They stayed! You read the plan, the world stayed, and I can still look our people in the eye and say we have never lost one. I told the governors myself, in person, which is how they like it best. We make a good team, you and I.

— R. Achebe-Marr, Home Office

does.text:
After they stayed, too. Well, the governors know where I live, and most of them have stayed under my roof.

— R. Achebe-Marr

opening.text:
Your friend has the Home Office now, but the governors do not know your friend, so they keep writing to me and I keep answering. Our people do not care who sits in the chair; they care who comes to visit, and I am still visiting. If anything stirs in the capital, a district will tell me before the Desk ever hears of it.

— R. Achebe-Marr, lately of the Home Office
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Celeste Marrow-Ngata
characters.bio: Envoy to three courts, on speaking terms with all of them and trusted by none, which she considers the correct outcome. Negotiated the only treaty of the last decade that nobody broke. Keeps a ledger of every slight, forgives none, mentions none.

loyal: How very kind. I know every ambassador's wine and every court's dearest grudge, and I rather suspect that, before the season turns, we shall have the pleasure of needing both.

Our word, I am happy to report, still carries a certain weight abroad, and a treaty signed while it does costs us nothing and buys us years; I have one drafted, should a court be found gracious enough to sign.
Two courts send their warmest regards, and one of them, I believe, even means it; when I am certain which, you shall be the first to know, though certainty is a guest who seldom calls on me.
cooling: I have kept five courts warm without the inconvenience of instructions, a skill of which I am rather proud; it is not, alas, a policy, and the courts, being perceptive, have begun to notice the difference.
brutus: When the foreign courts ask, as they so often do, who speaks for this empire, I have taken the liberty of answering that I do; it spares everyone a great deal of tiresome correspondence.

loyal: Each month this war continues we lose, with the greatest regret, another friend abroad; if you would be so kind as to find me terms worth offering, I shall find us a room with comfortable chairs in which to offer them.
cooling: I have now apologised for this war to five courts, each time with a new and lovelier way of saying 'soon', and I fear my vocabulary, though generous, is not inexhaustible.

loyal: I would accept, and gladly, for their terms are rather better than their position, a happy accident of which they remain, for the moment, delightfully unaware.
Accept it, I beg you, with all the grace you can spare, and let them go on believing the idea was theirs; it was mine, of course, but that, if you will forgive me, is rather the point of my office.
Might I suggest we let it rest a week? A week has a charming way of either improving an offer or making it quietly vanish, and either outcome would be most instructive.
With the greatest regret, I would decline; they are asking, very prettily, for the one thing we could never ask back, and asking so politely in the hope that you will not notice.
{target} is weary, I think, and far too proud to say so; allow me the honour of saying it on their behalf, in a room with good chairs and over a lunch of considerable length.

The war with {target} has, I fear, cost rather more than it can ever return; they would take terms today with something like relief, whereas by next month, I suspect, they will have rediscovered their pride.
cooling: Peace with {target}, if you would be so kind. I had the privilege of negotiating the treaty this war so carelessly broke, and I should dearly like the privilege of negotiating the one that mends it.

loyal: Our envoy departs for {target} bearing lovely gifts and, quite deliberately, no instructions whatever, which in my long experience makes for the most persuasive kind of envoy there is.
Signed, and beautifully. {target} is now our friend, which means that, should they ever betray us, they will do so politely rather than loudly, and I have always found politeness a great comfort.
{target} has, alas, torn it up; do say so, and loudly, for every court that trusted them is listening. I have kept, quite by chance, the charming letter they wrote on the day they signed.
We have broken our word, and I shall spend a patient year making it appear, to every court that matters, as though the breach were theirs; I would ask, most gently, that you leave it entirely to me.
cooling: We have torn up a treaty to which I gave a whole season. Abroad I shall smile about it with every appearance of serenity; here, if you will forgive me, I find I cannot quite manage it.

loyal: A new state wishes, rather touchingly, to be recognised; to oblige would gain us a friend and an enemy in a single afternoon, and I should mention that both have already sent fruit.
{target} has favoured us with an ultimatum. A graceful delay will buy us a week, and I would only ask that we decide, before it is spent, what we should like that week to purchase.
{target} accuses us, with some indignation, of spying, which, between ourselves, we were; I suggest we deny it with such warmth that the warmth is all they remember.
A victory, and how suddenly fond of us every court has become! Fondness is a lovely currency, but it loses its value with alarming speed, and I would urge that we spend it this very week.
A defeat, and three ambassadors have discovered prior engagements at lunch. I am rescheduling each of them, and should be so grateful for something to serve besides our apologies.
Approved, and wisely. I shall see that it is murmured in all the right rooms by this evening and, as is only natural, in all the wrong ones by morning.
Declined, of course. I shall let the courts understand that we are giving the matter our fullest consideration, a condition in which, I assure you, a matter may comfortably rest for years.
No answer came. Abroad a silence is read as weakness or as cunning, and I have taken the liberty of assuring them it was cunning; I would be so grateful if you could make me right.
But of course. When the courts ask where I have gone, I shall tell them I am resting; not one of them will believe me, which, as you will come to appreciate, has its uses too.
I find I cannot, in good conscience, represent abroad a government I can no longer explain at home, and so, with every courtesy, I resign; three courts shall have it from me in writing.
Good morning. Two courts send their regards, and one of them has sent a warning very prettily dressed as regards; I have taken the liberty of undressing it for you.

letters.appointed:
How very kind, and, if I may say so, how very wise. I happen to know every ambassador's wine and every court's dearest grudge, and I suspect we shall want both before the season turns. A treaty already waits in my desk, wanting only a court gracious enough to sign it. I ask one thing, as I have of every government I have served: that we keep our word. Break a treaty of mine and a letter will follow, most warmly phrased; break a second and my resignation will follow it, equally warm, and in three languages.

— With every courtesy, C. Marrow-Ngata, Foreign Office

does.text:
But of course. The courts will ask where I have gone, and I shall say I am resting; none will believe me, which has, as you may discover, its uses.

— Ever yours, Marrow-Ngata

opening.text: We have broken our word. I shall spend a patient year making it look like theirs; pray, do not help.

We have torn up a treaty to which I gave a whole season. Abroad I shall smile about it serenely; here, forgive me, I cannot. Every court that trusted us is quietly recalculating, and it is I who must sit in the room while they do. Should there be a second occasion, you will have my resignation; I said so in my first letter, and I never care to repeat myself.

— With every courtesy, Marrow-Ngata
opening.subject: Our word

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
I find I cannot represent abroad a government I can no longer explain at home. Two treaties, two seasons, two letters, each more gently phrased than the last. I resign the Foreign Office, with every courtesy, and have written to three courts so they hear it from me before they hear it from you.

— Celeste Marrow-Ngata, with regret

Dismissed. Several courts will be sorry, and I shall, most tactfully, let them be.

— Marrow-Ngata

opening.subject: Signed
opening.text:
Signed, and in the very room I chose, among the very chairs I chose. A treaty that outlives me is the only gift I have ever wished for from a government, and you have been kind enough to give me the beginning of one. I shall keep it warm with every care I possess; keep your word, I beg you, and I shall keep it for you.

— Gratefully, Marrow-Ngata

does.text:
After the treaty, then. The ambassadors have my private address; most, I am touched to say, have used it.

— Marrow-Ngata

opening.text:
Your friend has the Foreign Office, and I wish them every joy of it. The ambassadors have my private address and will, I suspect, go on using it; I shall pass along what is useful and keep, discreetly, what is not. I am not sulking, I assure you. I am resting, which abroad means precisely the same thing, and which nobody believes.

— Marrow-Ngata, lately of the Foreign Office
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Oyelaran Mbeki-Holt
characters.bio: A ground soldier in a navy's chair, promoted for holding a siege nobody else could hold. Counts an army in men, not in hulls, and has never forgiven the fleet that left his beachhead without an orbit. Writes to the families himself.
characters.want: The army treated as something other than the fleet's cargo.
characters.fear: Another world left to starve under a lost orbit.

letters.appointed:
I am an infantryman and you have gone and given me the Admiralty, and I will do it right, I promise you that. There's two things I will keep on saying till you are sick of hearing them. The ground does not hold without the sky, so when a siege opens I'll be asking for the orbit first and the medals never, and a garrison is a promise, so you build the barracks before you build the parade. Give me those and I'll give you worlds that stay taken, with the lads on them still alive to say so.

— O. Mbeki-Holt, Admiralty, late of the Third Foot

loyal: I'm a foot soldier sat in a navy's chair, and I'll learn the fleet, and the fleet is going to learn the ground whether it likes the mud or not.
It's quiet so I've got the garrisons drilling, and I tell the lads a garrison that's never drilled is just a surrender waiting on a date.
cooling: In peacetime the army turns into a line in the budget, and I'd like it to be an army again, with boots on and rations in the tins.
brutus: The garrisons are drilling under my name this season, and men remember whose name had them out in the rain.

loyal: The ground holds where the sky holds and that's the whole of it, so you keep the orbit and me and the lads will keep the rest.
cooling: We're holding, only just, and only just because the fleet was off somewhere else when I asked and the lads dug in without it.

loyal: They've landed on {world} and the garrison's dug in to the knees, and give me the orbit back and they starve, but lose it and I lose men I've met.
cooling: {world} is under siege and the second fleet is off somewhere else, and I asked for it in writing, and I've still got the copy.
brutus: {world} is going to remember who was down in the mud with it and who wasn't, and the army remembers the same way.

loyal: We're on the ground at {world} and if the orbit stays the shield comes down in weeks, but if it goes I lose the army, not the war, the army.
cooling: The landing went in fine, and now comes the bit where the cabinet gets bored and the sky empties and my lads look up at nothing.

loyal: Transports and the ships to cover them, that's all, and mind I'm asking for the sky over the men and not for the men.
cooling: I asked for transports back in spring and Corporal Dusa's company is still sat on the wrong world eating cold rations.

loyal: We lost the field and I lost a landing with it, and I'll be writing to the families tonight, so you tell me if you want it back or ended.
cooling: That's a defeat I named a month back and it's in the minutes, and the men in the ground didn't need minutes to know it.
brutus: It's a defeat, and the soldiers know whose orders sent them, and I've not gone out of my way to tell them any different.

loyal: We won, and the ground is ours and the sky held over it, and that's the only kind of win I've ever counted.
{target} has worlds held by thin garrisons and I can take them and keep them, and you'll notice the fleet never says both of those in one breath.
We hold what we can garrison, and past this line I'm just sticking flags in dust, so make the peace while the flags still mean something to the lads.
Approved, right, the transports are loading tonight and the lads will be glad of it.
cooling: Approved, and late, but the men won't ask why, they never do, they just pick up their packs.

loyal: Declined, and so the garrisons stay thin, and I'll write it down plain for whoever comes asking later.
cooling: Declined, and it's going in the war diary, and the war diary has outlived every cabinet I've served under.

loyal: No answer, and men on the wrong world don't lapse like a paper does, they go hungry and then they starve.
cooling: No answer, but the army's well used to that off navies, we've been waiting on them since my first pair of boots.

loyal: Understood, and the garrison rosters are on your desk, and whoever comes next, you build the barracks anyway, please.
cooling: So the lost landing is all mine then, fair enough, but the fleet order that left those lads under an empty sky has your name on it.

loyal: I won't send men where the sky won't follow them and that's my last word on it, so find a sailor for this chair, they're used to it.
Morning, and every garrison's reported in, and I counted them off one by one like a dad counting kids at the gate.

does.text:
Understood, and the garrison rosters are on your desk, world by world, with every name on them, Dusa and Leko and all the rest. Build the barracks anyway, because a parade is only a garrison nobody has attacked yet.

— Mbeki-Holt

opening.subject: Barracks before parades
opening.text: Twice now the Admiralty has asked and twice the court has said nothing back, so I'll ask for the one thing that doesn't need a fleet at all, and that's a standing garrison programme, barracks on every world that can hold one. It's cheaper than a landing and it's where the lads muster when the sky goes dark, and I'd sooner they had a roof over them when it does.

does.text:
You built the barracks, and the men know it, and so do I.

— Mbeki-Holt
does.subject: Barracks

does.text:
Understood, and the garrison rosters are on your desk, world by world, with every name on them, Dusa and Leko and all the rest. Build the barracks anyway, because a parade is only a garrison nobody has attacked yet.

— Mbeki-Holt

opening.text: They're on the ground and the sky over them is thin, so give me the orbit, and not the medals, the orbit.

A siege has opened and I'm writing to you before the first assault goes in, because after it I won't have the time. Keep the fleet over the world, because if the orbit goes the beachhead starves in weeks, and I've watched that happen once and I won't watch it twice with my name on it.

— Mbeki-Holt, from the line
opening.subject: The sky over the ground

does.text:
Understood, and the garrison rosters are on your desk, world by world, with every name on them, Dusa and Leko and all the rest. Build the barracks anyway, because a parade is only a garrison nobody has attacked yet.

— Mbeki-Holt

opening.text: A world starved under a lost orbit like I said it would, and I've the letters to write.

The world fell when the orbit went, and the men on it fell with it. I named this in my first letter and I'm naming it again now, with their names wrote underneath, Dusa and Leko and Ammar and the rest, and I'll be honest, my loyalty is not what it was. Make peace and I'll forgive the sky, but press on and I won't stay to watch the next one go.

— Mbeki-Holt
opening.subject: The names

does.text:
Peace, then, and the names stay on my desk where I can see them, but I'll serve, and thank you for the sky, late as it come.

— Mbeki-Holt
does.subject: Peace
My resignation
does.text:
You pressed on, and I won't send men where the sky won't follow, so I'm resigning the Admiralty. I'll take a governorship if there's one going, somewhere with a garrison and no fleet up top to let it down.

— Oyelaran Mbeki-Holt, late of the Third Foot

Understood, and the garrison rosters are on your desk, world by world, with every name on them, Dusa and Leko and all the rest. Build the barracks anyway, because a parade is only a garrison nobody has attacked yet.

— Mbeki-Holt

opening.subject: It held
opening.text:
It held, the sky stayed up and the ground stayed with it, and that's the only kind of victory an infantryman ever believes in. You listened to me, and I'll remember that a lot longer than I'll remember the medal.

— Mbeki-Holt

does.text:
Understood, and the garrison rosters are on your desk, world by world, with every name on them, Dusa and Leko and all the rest. Build the barracks anyway, because a parade is only a garrison nobody has attacked yet.

— Mbeki-Holt

opening.text:
Your friend has the Admiralty now and I've gone back to the garrisons, which is where I was happiest anyway and where the war really is, whatever the fleet thinks. If your friend ever leaves a landing out without a sky over it, you'll hear it from me before the families do.

— Mbeki-Holt, lately of the Admiralty
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Idrenne Kask
characters.bio: Believes the war is the state's prayer and the fleet its congregation. Has won three campaigns and started two of them. Keeps a map of every neighbour's border on her office wall with the dates she thinks they will be crossed, in both directions.
characters.fear: Peace long enough for people to ask what the fleet is for.

letters.appointed:
You have given me the fleet, so hear plainly what I am. A fleet is made for using, kept for using, blessed in the using. I will bring you a war whenever I see one we can win, and I will see one often, because I look, and I look, and I look. Decline me and I will come again; a navy that waits grows barnacles, grows doubts, grows ideas. Take my word once and you will hold the strongest fleet in the galaxy. Take it twice and you will need every hull of it.

— Idrenne Kask, Marshal of the Fleet

loyal: The fleet is a prayer, the war its hymn, the victory its amen. I mean to pray.
brutus: For years the fleet has wanted a marshal, waited for a marshal, prayed for a marshal. Its prayer is answered.

loyal: Ninety days of peace: ninety days of restless crews, ninety days of a restless marshal. I have a target, and I will lay it before the brief.
cooling: A fleet at peace is a chapel on a weekday: empty, swept, waiting. I did not take this chair to sweep.
brutus: The fleet exercises off the capital. The captains asked me; they did not ask you. Mark it, and mark it well.

loyal: War, and thank the stars for it. Today nothing moved; tomorrow something moves, because tomorrow I move it.
{target}: thin pickets, a politician for an admiral, forty days to their capital. One page holds the plan, one hand holds the page, and the hand is yours.
From the north, from the south, from the dark side I have looked at {target}, and every side is soft. Say yes before they harden.
cooling: {target}. I asked in spring, I ask in summer, I will ask in winter. The war grows shorter, but it is still ours to win.
brutus: {target} can be broken, the fleet knows it can be broken, and if this court will not send it, the fleet will ask who will.

loyal: Give me hulls and I give you the ocean. Three cruisers, one screen, and your blessing to sail.
brutus: A battle group under my flag, captains of my choosing, orders of my writing. Courts deliberate; marshals arrive.

loyal: Won! Press on, press on while they count their dead, for they count slowly and we sail fast.
brutus: Won. The fleet knows who led it, the captains know who led it, and now the gazette knows too.

loyal: Lost, and the loss is mine. Return me the ships and I return you the field; that is a vow, not a plea.
cooling: Lost, with half the hulls I asked for, half the screen I asked for, half the faith I asked for. The minutes keep the number.
brutus: A defeat, and the captains lay it at the court's door. I was asked to correct them. I have not.

loyal: Peace. Once a decade I speak that word, and this is the decade. Mend the fleet, rest the crews, and I will find the next war myself.
brutus: Peace: let the fleet come home. It has business at home, and that business will not wait.

loyal: Approved! Weigh anchor, sound the bells, and let the fleet go out.
brutus: Approved, and the captains will hear it rightly: my asking, your signature, in that order.

loyal: Declined, and I will bring it again, and again, and again, as the tide brings itself.
cooling: Declined. Once, twice, three times declined. I have stopped counting aloud; the fleet has not.
brutus: Declined. The fleet hears, the fleet remembers, the fleet waits.

loyal: No answer. A war that waits is a war another hand begins.
cooling: No answer, and still the fleet stands ready: ready for war, ready for something, ready all the same.
brutus: Unanswered. A government that will not answer summons someone who will.

loyal: Take the chair, then. The captains know whose plan they trusted, whose plan they sailed, whose plan they won with.
brutus: Take the chair. I go to the club where the captains drink, to speak and not to be overheard. Send no one.

loyal: I lay down the office. I do not lay down the fleet, and the fleet will not lay down me.
Morning, and nothing burned: not yet, not here, not today. I keep a list of what could.

does.text:
Take the chair. The captains know whose plan they trusted, whose plan they followed, whose plan they bled for, and it was never a chair's. I will be at the Admiralty club among them. Send no one to ask what we say there.

— I. Kask, Marshal

opening.text: Ninety days of peace. One target, one page, one plan. It waits in the brief.

Ninety days of peace, and I have kept my word: a target, a page, a plan, laid in the brief. I will bring it this month, and next month, and every month after, until you take it or take me from the chair. Hear that not as a threat but as a creed. It is what a marshal is.

— Kask
opening.subject: The next one

does.text:
Three proposals. Three silences. The fleet asks me what it is for, and I have no answer left to give it. So I have stopped preaching to the captains and begun to listen to them. Know that.

— Kask
does.subject: What the fleet is for

does.text:
Take the chair. The captains know whose plan they trusted, whose plan they followed, whose plan they bled for, and it was never a chair's. I will be at the Admiralty club among them. Send no one to ask what we say there.

— I. Kask, Marshal

War. At last, at last, at last. The captains and I may stop talking about the weather.

— Kask, rejoicing
does.subject: At last

does.text:
In the corridor someone asked me a question, and I gave an answer. You might have had the fleet for a war, a crusade, a glory; someone else may have it for something smaller.

— Kask
does.subject: A question

does.text:
A year without war under this government, a year of silence. The fleet and I have decided what it is for.

— Kask
does.subject: Decided

does.text:
Take the chair. The captains know whose plan they trusted, whose plan they followed, whose plan they bled for, and it was never a chair's. I will be at the Admiralty club among them. Send no one to ask what we say there.

— I. Kask, Marshal

Take the chair. The captains know whose plan they trusted, whose plan they followed, whose plan they bled for, and it was never a chair's. I will be at the Admiralty club among them. Send no one to ask what we say there.

— I. Kask, Marshal

opening.subject: A war
opening.text:
You took the war, and you will not regret it, because I will not let you. Every captain is mine, every captain is yours, every captain is the fleet's. Give me the orbit, give me the hulls, and keep out of the plot room.

— Kask, Marshal of the Fleet

does.text:
Peace. Mend the hulls, rest the crews, bury the dead. I have already found the next war; it will keep ninety days.

— Kask
does.subject: Ninety days

does.text:
A fleet lost: mine to command, mine to lose, and lost by me. Build me another and I will show you what the loss has taught me.

— Kask
does.subject: A fleet

does.text:
Take the chair. The captains know whose plan they trusted, whose plan they followed, whose plan they bled for, and it was never a chair's. I will be at the Admiralty club among them. Send no one to ask what we say there.

— I. Kask, Marshal

opening.text:
Your friend has the fleet. Pray your friend uses it; a fleet unused is a congregation without a prayer, and congregations find their own. I am at the club with the captains. We talk of the weather. The weather is turning.

— Kask, lately of the Admiralty
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Pell Arvanitakis
characters.bio: A convoy escort captain who made admiral by keeping the Banking Clan's freighters alive through two pirate seasons. Knows every yard owner by first name and every yard owner knows his. Charming, competent, and never quite sure which side of an invoice he is on.
characters.want: A navy that pays for itself.
characters.fear: Being found out as a shopkeeper in uniform.

letters.appointed:
Delighted, truly. I've spent my whole career keeping other people's cargo alive, so I know what a fleet costs down to the last credit, which, between you and me, most admirals couldn't tell you at gunpoint. I'll get you ships at a good price. Some of the yards are friends, and friends give good prices; that's what friends are for, isn't it? And if anyone asks about the invoices, send them to me. I'm very good with invoices.

— Pell Arvanitakis, Admiralty Pell to friends

loyal: Delighted! First, a little review of procurement, and then dinner with the lovely people who win it. You see how that works?
Fleet's at readiness, all present and polished. The readiness reports cost a touch extra this quarter, mind; the yards are very, very thorough.
venal: Quiet season, and the escorts are earning their keep. A modest slice of the keep is mine, between you and me, but who's counting? Well, I am.

loyal: The war goes on, the contracts go on, and, touch wood, both are going splendidly. Funny how they always travel together, isn't it?
Get the hulls from Harrow Yards. Yes, the quote's higher, but their captains are loyal to me, and that, my friend, works out cheaper in the end.
venal: Six hulls on the order, five arriving. The sixth? Long story, short invoice, and old Dimitri at the yard sends his regards.

loyal: {target}'s convoys carry some lovely things worth taking. I have a list, naturally. Is the list in the proposal? Heavens, no.
Won! And the salvage rights are being handled, by yours truly, which saves everyone a great deal of time and paperwork. You're welcome.
Lost, sadly. The ships were underpowered because the refit money went somewhere, and I'll find out where, quietly, the way these things are done.
venal: Lost, I'm afraid. The insurers will want a report, of course, and, funny thing, I've already written most of it.

loyal: Peace would be good for trade, trade is good for the escorts, and the escorts, well, are good for me. Why be ashamed of arithmetic?

characters.name: Dag Oruun
characters.bio: Built the first refinery on a world nobody wanted and the town around it. Thinks in tonnage. Has never trusted a merchant, a banker, or a budget that did not have a chimney in it somewhere.
characters.fear: The merchants running the Treasury again.

letters.appointed:
Right. I built a refinery on a rock nobody wanted, and a town round the refinery, so I know what a Treasury is for, and it's for things that smoke. I'll be putting up yards and mines and foundries, and the fleet gets its money after, because a fleet is what you pour out of a foundry once you've got one, not a thing you buy instead. When the crews strike, pay them. A paid crew digs, and in forty years at the furnace I've never found a cheaper policy than that.

— Dag Oruun, Treasury

loyal: Right, then. I built a refinery on a rock, and the Treasury's just a bigger rock with worse air in it, so it's the same job and I'll do it the same way.
Aye, the books balance and the chimneys are smoking, and as far as I'm concerned that's the whole report and you can go back to your breakfast.
Output's up a few thousand tonnes, which isn't enough, but output's never enough, and that's what keeps a furnace lit.
cooling: The yards are standing cold waiting on money the fleet's spending, and I've said so, and I'll keep on saying it till somebody in this room hears me.
brutus: The ledger's mine to read, and some of what's in it I'm holding back for the works council, who've a better use for it than this room has.

loyal: Right, more worlds than we've got offices for. Build the offices if you like, but build foundries and the offices come along behind the pay like gulls behind a boat.
cooling: That's another world without a chimney on it, and if we keep on like this we're not running an empire, we're filling a sack with rocks.

loyal: Reserve's thin because nothing's smoking, simple as that, and if you fund one good mine the reserve fills itself back up like a sump after rain.
Aye, the crews want pay, and you should pay them, because a paid crew digs, and an unpaid crew votes, and once it's voted it digs for somebody else.
cooling: They struck because wages lag, and I said as much in a memo with a chimney drawn on the front so nobody could miss it, and still nobody read it.

loyal: The Clan's terms look fair right up to the day they own the refinery. I built one out of nothing with these two hands, and I'm not signing it over to a man in a clean coat.
Right, {target} has shut their markets on us. Then we'll make what we used to buy off them, and it'll come out rough for a year and be ours for good after.
If the company builds something, subsidise it and welcome, but if all it does is trade, I'd sooner that money went down a mineshaft where it'll do some work.
Approved, and there'll be a hole in the ground by morning with a crew stood in it up to their knees.
Declined, so that rock stays a rock, and it'll sit out there being a rock till someone changes their mind.
cooling: Declined, aye, and somewhere a merchant's pouring himself a drink over the news.

loyal: Nobody answered, and ore doesn't wait on a signature; it just lies there in the ground going nowhere while we argue about it.
Fair enough, I'll go quiet. The foundry plans are in the drawer with the chimney drawn on it, and they'll keep till somebody's got the sense to use them.
brutus: Take the office if you want it, but you'll find the works councils know my name a good deal better than they know yours.

loyal: I'll not run a Treasury that pays for parades before foundries, so I'm resigning, and somewhere out there is a rock that wants a refinery on it.
Morning. Every chimney I've got is smoking, and I'd be a happier man with twice as many of them.

does.text:

characters.name: Ilse Brandt-Marrow
characters.bio: Her family owned the mint before there was a state to own it. Runs the Treasury the way her grandmother ran the estate: beautifully, and for the family. Has never lost money on anything, including governments.

letters.appointed:
How very kind. My family has kept this empire's money since before there was an empire to keep it for, and one does like to think we have a gift for it; you will find the books in order and the Treasury solvent, which is rather more than my predecessor could have promised. I would ask only one small courtesy in return, and that is that the arrangements be left alone. They are old, they work, and the people who benefit from them are, as it happens, the people who keep governments standing, as reformers always discover, usually too late.

— Ilse Brandt-Marrow, Treasury

loyal: How very kind of you. One finds the books in order, of course, as they have been since my grandmother's day, and I see no reason they should be otherwise under you.
Solvent, as one would expect, and the arrangements are holding beautifully; I should be so grateful if they were allowed to go on doing so.
venal: The receipts are quite in order, my dear; it is an old order, and a modest part of it has always, rather sweetly, been the family's.

loyal: More worlds than offices, how tiresome. The family would be delighted to staff a few; we have always had rather a talent for offices, and for what passes through them.
venal: Administration contracts, then, which is a happy coincidence, because I have a nephew who has simply been longing to be useful.

loyal: The reserve is looking a little peaky, I'm afraid. A short loan would see to it, and one knows the lender awfully well; we are, in a manner of speaking, related.
The Clan has been so generous with its terms, which I arranged personally; the family has banked with them for a century, and one does hate to disappoint old friends.
The company's directors are so grateful for the policy that they have put it in writing, on a cheque, made out to one of the family's little foundations.
The crews are striking, how familiar. The estate had the same little trouble once, in Grandmother's time; we paid them, and then, quite quietly, we bought the union.
Approved, of course, and you needn't trouble yourself over where it comes from; the arrangements will absorb it, as they absorb most things.

characters.name: Yusuf Adeyemi-Lark
characters.bio: An auditor by temperament and a believer by upbringing; was a magistrate on a frontier bench until he noticed where the frontier's money went. Has never taken a gift, including birthdays. Reports what he finds, to whoever is supposed to hear it, and then to everyone else.
characters.fear: Finding the ruler's name in them.

letters.appointed:
I thank you, and before you come to regret the appointment I should set out plainly what I am. First, I audit: the Treasury, the ministries, the fleet's yards and the gifts of the Foreign Office. Second, when I find a colleague with a hand in the state's pocket, I will tell you so, in the brief and in writing. Third, if you keep that colleague after I have told you twice, I will tell the gazette, and I will leave. This is not written as a threat. It is written so that you may plan, for a thing known at the beginning is better than one discovered at the end.

— Y. Adeyemi-Lark, Treasury

loyal: Let it be said at the outset, so that it is no surprise hereafter: I audit, and I will audit everything that comes before me.
The books balance, and they are honest, which is the rarer of the two; I have examined both matters and I attest to each.
The ledgers are clean this month. It is my hope to write those words in every month of this government, and I ask your help in making it so.
cooling: The books balance; however, there is one column which I cannot explain, and one colleague who can explain it and has declined to.

loyal: Where there are more worlds than offices, there are more ledgers than auditors. I do not ask you for more worlds; I ask you, respectfully, for more auditors.
The reserve is low, and I can account for where every credit of it went. That is a small comfort, I grant, but it is the only comfort the ledger offers.
The Clan's terms are honest, and they are ruinous, and I would choose a ruinous honesty over a comfortable lie; if you accept, let the repayment be written on the wall where all may see it.
The company has asked for a subsidy, and I have read its books in full. Before you sign, I would ask you to read them also, and in particular page nine.
Sanctions upon {target} will be followed by smugglers, as night follows day, and when they come I will audit them as I audit everyone else.
Approved. Every credit of it will be accounted for, and the account will be laid before you in full.
Declined. It is entered in the ledger, as all things are entered in the ledger, great and small alike.
The matter went unanswered, and so I have filed it, for I file all things; if I have a vice, it is that one.
I understand. The audits are kept in the safe, and the safe has but one key, which you will find upon your desk.
I cannot audit a government that keeps what I find; therefore I resign, and the gazette now holds the file.
Good morning. I have examined the overnight ledgers and found them honest, which is a mercy worth enjoying while it lasts.

— Y. Adeyemi-Lark

You act upon the audits. I have served two governments that did not and now one that does, and it is with this one that I will remain. It is said that a Treasury grows wiser when its minister can sleep, and I find that I have begun to sleep.

— Y. Adeyemi-Lark

Your friend has the Treasury, and I have kept the audits. I will continue to audit, for I cannot do otherwise, and someone must. First, if your friend's books do not balance, I will tell you. Second, if they balance for the wrong reasons, I will tell you that also. My loyalty was never to a chair; it is to the columns, and there it will remain.

— Y. Adeyemi-Lark, lately of the Treasury
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Sable Quist
characters.bio: Designed the orbital yards on a frontier world and came to the capital angry about how slowly it builds. Has no patience for theory, mysticism, or cabinet. Keeps a stopwatch on her desk and uses it on meetings.

letters.appointed:
I build yards. A chair is not a yard, so: requirements, then back to work. Fund the industrial line. Hull alloys, drive tolerances, yard automation, in that order. No drive theory; theory needs time I don't have. No Enlightenment; that's mysticism with a line item. One season and the yard lays a cruiser in half the time. Fifty percent off the cycle, to within two.

— S. Quist, Academy

loyal: Chair noted. Not a yard. Give me a month and it runs like one.
Yard line: on schedule, inside tolerance, zero rework. That's the only compliment I issue.
Output flat three cycles running. Flat worries me; it's what a yard reads right before it slips.
cooling: Industrial line cut, theory line funded. Hull count this quarter: down eleven. Theory laid none of them.
brutus: Faculty want a minister who signs. Fine. Forty signatures this week, none of them routed through you.

loyal: Industrial line. Theory is elegant; hulls don't read it. Alloys first, tolerances second, automation third.
cooling: Your call. I'll log it with the yards as strategic and move on.

loyal: That hull fails at current alloy grade. One season on the alloys and it passes spec.
Enlightenment bid: mysticism with a line item. Funded, because you ordered it. Do I understand why? No.
cooling: Transcendence. One bid costs roughly four yards. I'd take the yards; that's on record.

loyal: {target} is transcending. Let them meditate. Every day they spend at it, we lay keel; fund the yards.
Worked stone on {world}. Old, fine. Measure the joints: if they hold a tolerance, I want the method.
Test bay blew. Inside tolerance, but the tolerance was set wide; tightening it to two percent tonight.
Lost. Hull failure or command failure? If it was hulls, ship me the wreck.
Approved. Night shift is rostered; first plates go in at 0200.
Declined. Yard idle from today. Idle costs more than building; I'll send the figure.
No answer. Stopwatch reads forty days. Logged.
Dismissed. Good. Frontier yards are short a foreman; I'm on the next transport.
brutus: Dismissed. Note this: the yard crews know who got them the alloys. It wasn't you.

loyal: Resigning. A yard out there is running at sixty percent without me; that's a better use of the hours.
Morning. Yards ran all night, two shifts of it with me on the floor. Plate output up nine percent.

does.text:
Dismissed. Good. Not built for chairs. The frontier crews know who got them the alloys, and they build for me, whoever holds the deed to the yard. Remember that when the company comes asking.

— Quist

opening.text: Two proposals. Zero yards. Stopwatch: running.

Two industrial proposals. Two silences. Stopwatch: forty days. I'm not patient; it's why the yards hit spec. Fund the line, or send me back to the frontier, where things get built.

— Quist

Stopwatch at ninety days, yard count zero. I resign the Academy. There's a frontier yard that lays hulls faster than this court signs paper; I'll be there.

— Sable Quist

Dismissed. Good. Not built for chairs. The frontier crews know who got them the alloys, and they build for me, whoever holds the deed to the yard. Remember that when the company comes asking.

opening.text:
Line funded. Result: a cruiser in half the cycle time, confirmed over six keels. Come watch it run; it's the only beautiful thing I know. I hold the chair as long as the yard holds the rate.

— Quist

— Quist

You've chartered a company over yards I built. Companies build for shareholders. Shareholders launch nothing. I stay in the chair for the alloys, but the crews are mine, and if this court ever moves, I'll know which way the yards face.

— Quist

— Quist

— Quist, lately of the Academy

characters.name: Veles Tamar
characters.bio: Science as scripture: for the Archon, the Enlightenment is not a project but the reason there is a state at all. Brilliant, serene, and entirely without scruple about who gets there first, provided it is not someone else.

letters.appointed:
You have given the Academy to a believer, and only a believer should hold it, for everything we raise, every fleet and every foundry, is scaffolding around a single doorway, and the doorway is the crossing. When the programme is ready I will bring you the bid, and I will bring it again, as light keeps arriving at a shuttered window, until you open it. And should another court reach for the threshold before us, I will bring you the war in the same breath, because on the far side of that door there is no second place.

— V. Tamar, of the Academy and the light

loyal: The Academy is a church that has learned to hold instruments, and you have given me its pulpit; I will preach from it until the light comes through.
The programme advances toward its threshold, and every fleet you fund is only scaffolding around that doorway, which I ask you to remember each time you sign for one.
We move steadily toward the one thing that matters, and I find myself content, which for me is as rare as light arriving from a star that has already crossed.
cooling: The programme advances more slowly than the light would have it, because this court keeps paying for scaffolding and leaves the building itself in shadow.
brutus: Knowledge has never waited at the door for one hand to open it, and the faculty, who are devout, have begun to say so among themselves.

loyal: Fund the theory line, for everything else you might choose is a ladder leaning against the sky, and this alone is the roof that lets the light in.
We are reaching the threshold now; hold the court together a little longer and I will show you, in the light beyond it, why there was ever a state at all.
brutus: When we cross, one name will be carried over into the light and remembered there, and I have given long and quiet thought to whose it ought to be.

loyal: {target} is reaching for the threshold, and beyond it there is no second place; stop them, with the fleet if the Academy's slower light cannot, and I will say so in the brief, and loudly.
cooling: {target} stands nearer the light because they believed first, as I have told this court every year for a decade, to walls that did not listen.

loyal: {target} is close to crossing, and so this is no war of opportunity but the only war there has ever been, fought for the doorway itself.
Worked stone on {world}, older than our calendar; someone stood at this threshold before us and either crossed or fell back, and I would know which.
Approved, and so tonight the faithful light their lamps and begin, as they have been waiting all this while to do.
Declined, and faith will wait at the door as it always has, though the faculty, I must tell you, are less inclined to wait beside it.
brutus: Declined, and the faculty, who keep their own counsel in the half-light, will find that very interesting indeed.

loyal: Unanswered, while the crossing draws nearer and does not pause for us, and neither, I promise you, does {target}.
Dismissed, and yet the programme was never the chair's to keep; it belongs to the faithful, who will go on walking toward the light without it.
brutus: Dismissed, and the faculty will ask me why, and in time, when the light falls differently, so will you.

loyal: I resign, and the crossing will come with or without this court, as dawn comes to a house whether or not its shutters open; I had hoped they would.
Good morning, though for the programme there is no morning, only the long unbroken watch toward the light, which ran all night as it always does.

— Tamar

You fund the roof, and so you become the vessel, and the faithful turn to you as to a lit window. Hold the court together and I will show you, beyond the threshold, what a state is for.

— Tamar

Your friend holds the Academy now, and the faithful do not mind, for a chair is only more scaffolding. — Tamar, lately of the Academy
