characters.name: Corwin Ashby-Dolores
characters.bio: Patents instead of papers. Turned a university department into a licensing house and the licensing house into a seat at cabinet. Believes knowledge is property and property is safest in his name.

letters.appointed:
Delighted, and thank you. A word on the arrangement, since clarity up front saves considerable legal spend later. The Academy's discoveries vest in the state; the associated patents vest in the inventors, and I am, as it happens, inventor of record on a meaningful portion of the portfolio. This is standard practice and broadly in line with peer courts. I intend to run an Academy that is productive, profitable and, subject to the usual exclusions, value-accretive to the empire, where the bulk of the profit will remain.

— C. Ashby-Dolores, Academy (without prejudice)

loyal: Delighted to accept. For the record, patents remain with the inventor of record, and I hold, without prejudice, several.
The Academy delivered a productive and, this quarter, profitable result; the profit is allocated predominantly in-house, which is to say, to us.
venal: Research continues on schedule, a portion of it under private engagement; the clients value discretion, and discretion, I find, is a billable service.

loyal: My recommendation is the applied line: applications are licensable and theory is not, which explains, I think, why nobody funds it.
The company is seeking a subsidy plus a licence, and I have taken the liberty of drafting the licence on favourable terms; favourable to whom is a detail for the schedules.
Fascinating artefacts, and I have had them appraised; privately, you understand, under an appraisal methodology that is itself, I am pleased to say, patent-protected.
{target}'s programme is ahead of ours, but their lead scientist is, I am reliably informed, available for acquisition; so, in a sense, is the Academy, and I would rather we were the buyer.
There has been a containment event, attributable to equipment that was second-hand despite being invoiced as new; the matter has been referred for review to the parties who issued the invoice.
Approved, thank you; the supplier is a valued partner of mine, so delivery should be prompt and, I expect, competitively priced.
Declined, noted; the private clients, I should mention, are rarely so reticent, and their engagement letters remain open.
The proposal lapsed unanswered, and the supplier has applied a holding fee, which on review I consider entirely reasonable.
Understood. The patents depart with me, per the arrangement, which was always the arrangement and to which I would refer you in writing.
I tender my resignation; the licences are mine, the discoveries are yours, and the allocation between the two is, regrettably, a matter for counsel.
Good morning. Licensing receipts settled overnight, a portion of them remitted to the Treasury in accordance with the agreed schedule.

— Ashby-Dolores, without prejudice

— Ashby-Dolores, lately of the Academy

characters.name: Ottilie Ferrand
characters.bio: Ran the embassy in a rival court for a decade and its secrets for longer. Came home with a grudge the size of a treaty and a file on everyone she dined with. Charming at table, patient as stone, and never once forgetful.

letters.appointed:
Thank you for the Desk. I bring you the one thing my predecessor lacked, which is ten years inside another court, at its table and in its archives, long enough to know which of its ministers lies and which merely forgets. I will propose operations against that court early and often, as one orders the best dish before the kitchen runs out. Should you make peace with them, I will serve the peace with every grace I possess, and I will keep the file open, because peace is a pause between courses and the file, mon cher, is a decade.

— O. Ferrand, the Desk

loyal: I spent ten years at their table, and by the third I could tell you which fork each of them lied with.
Two networks abroad and one at home, all as quiet as a well-run dining room, which is precisely how I prefer the abroad to be.
Nothing to report, which tells me they have learned to be careful, a virtue they never once displayed over the cheese.
cooling: I would gladly tell you more, if only the cabinet took a few fewer suppers with ambassadors who never pay for their own wine.
brutus: I keep every file, you understand, even the charming little one on this government's dinners, which reads rather better than its policies.

loyal: Their network sits inside our ministries, and I know its handler, having sat opposite them through three winters of very bad soup; give me the authority and I will clear the table tonight.
{target} kept a network inside the Admiralty until four this morning, and I know their handler's taste in wine well enough to name the replacement before the month is out.
They have caught our hand in {target}'s pocket, so deny it warmly; I trained their counter-intelligence myself, and was careful to leave out everything that matters.
An officer of perfect loyalty was asked about a change at the head of the table, and the name of the one who asked is in the file; you dined with them this week.
cooling: There is talk of a plot, and I gave you the name last month between the soup and the fish, though I gather you were attending to the fish.
brutus: Rumours of a plot, nothing anyone could serve; I shall go on looking, at the tables of my own choosing.

loyal: A treaty with {target}, then, and I shall serve it as one serves a guest one dislikes, keeping the file open, since a treaty is only the pause between courses.
cooling: A treaty with the court whose table I sat at for ten years, and of course I shall smile, as I smiled at them then, all through the meal.

loyal: Your minister of {portfolio} has been dining with {target}'s ambassador, and I know precisely what that ambassador serves after the main course; do act before dessert.
It is tonight, and I have their names and know which rooms they will use, having used those rooms myself; tell me only which door you would like closed.
Approved, how kind; the operation was plated before you asked, for the Desk, under me, is never late to table.
Declined, of course, though the file stays open, files being like old guests, whose only virtue is that they never quite leave.
Unanswered, which I shall take as you mean it, since silence at table is a course of its own and frequently the most eloquent.
Understood; the files stay in the safe and the combination is with the Interior minister, so do change it, and while you are about it, change the wine.
I cannot protect a government that keeps dining with the very people I spent ten years learning to read, and so I resign; do lock the safe behind me.
Good morning; you were followed yesterday, by one of theirs this time, and I would know that walk across any ballroom in the galaxy.

does.text:
Understood. The files stay in the safe and the combination is with the Interior minister; do change it. I have kept one file, my own, because I wrote it and nobody else should read it. Good luck with the ambassadors; I know their menus, and what follows dessert.

— Ferrand

You have signed with a court I know far better than you do, and I will serve the treaty faithfully, as a good hostess serves a guest she would not have invited. I will also keep the file, because treaties are pauses and files are decades. I ask only one courtesy: do not ask me to close it, for I should have to refuse, and I would so much rather not refuse you.

— Ferrand

does.text:
The treaty is broken, as I said over the first course, and the file never left the table. Shall we begin?

— Ferrand
does.subject: As I said

does.text:
An alliance with them is a dish I cannot serve; I spent ten years learning why. I have written to their rebels, who remember my hospitality kindly. This is the one disloyalty I shall ever commit, and I commit it in my own hand, so that you need never wonder whose it was.

— Ferrand

Your friend has the Desk. I have handed over the safe and the networks and kept the dinners, which were never the state's to begin with. I shall go on listening at tables, since it is what I am for; if your friend misses something I will tell you, and if your friend is something, I will tell you that before the coffee.

— Ferrand, lately of the Desk
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Tomasz Ilyen
characters.bio: Confessor to the previous ruler, which means he has heard everything and repeated none of it, until now. Took the Desk because nobody else would hear confessions without using them. Refuses crackdowns the way other men refuse drink.

letters.appointed:
Brother Tomasz, at your service, and at the Desk, which surprises me as much as you. For twelve years I have heard this court's confessions; I will use none of them, only what I hear from now on, and only to keep the state honest. A shepherd once handed a sword used it to clear briars, and I mean to be that shepherd. I will not run a crackdown. Order one and I will tell you so; order two and I will tell the Interior minister what I think of you, which is a kind of confession too.

— T. Ilyen, the Desk

loyal: I have spent my life hearing confessions, and now I find the Desk is only a confessional that happens to keep accounts.
The court's souls are in order this month, and the Desk's files and the chapel's book, for once, tell the same story.
There is nothing to report, and I give thanks for it, because in a month like this one, nothing is a small grace.
cooling: I hear more truth at the altar rail than at the cabinet table, and I say it with sorrow, as a word about the table and not the rail.

loyal: There is a foreign hand inside the ministries, and I will find it. I will not hurt it; I will sit with it and listen, and that, in the end, is harder to bear.
A crackdown. I will not run it, though the Desk may run it without me; and if a second is ordered, I must carry it to the Interior minister as a sin, and I will grieve to do so.
cooling: A crackdown, and I did warn you once, softly, as I warn everyone I love.

loyal: Someone came to me and confessed they had been sounded out. I have the name of the one who did the sounding, and I give it to you with a heavy heart and a quiet conscience.
A campaign of lies in the gazette. I do not ask that the gazette be true, for no one could; I ask only that we not be the hand that makes it false.
Your minister of {portfolio} has been writing to {target}, and told me so under the seal of confession. I break that seal with sorrow, because a state has a soul too, and it is in danger.
It is tonight. The names came to me in the chapel and I give them to you now, and afterwards I will kneel and pray for all of you, theirs and ours alike.
Approved. It will be done gently, because under me gentleness is the only doctrine the Desk keeps.
Declined. I will go on listening, as I always have, for no door was ever built that closes on a listener.
Unanswered. A silence, too, is a kind of confession, and I have set it down beside the others.
Understood. The chapel stays open, and so does the Desk's safe; I never locked it, for there was nothing inside I would be ashamed for you to see.
I must resign, my child. A confessor cannot serve a state that makes sinners of its servants, but I will hear you still, whenever you come.
Good morning. Three souls came to me before breakfast, and not one of them spoke of you. I pray it stays that way.

does.text:
Understood. The chapel is open, and so is the safe; I never locked it, for there was nothing in it to be ashamed of. If you wish to talk, I am there most evenings, as are, you may like to know, a good many of your ministers.

— Ilyen

opening.text: A crackdown, as I warned. The second I will not run, whatever is asked.

You ordered the guard against your own people. I did not run it; the Desk ran it around me, as water runs around a stone. I will say this once, as I say most things: a second crackdown, and I carry what I know to the Interior minister as a sin against the state. I would far rather hear your confession than make your report. The choice is yours, as it nearly always is.

— Ilyen
opening.subject: A sin

does.text:
A second crackdown. I have gone to the Interior minister with what I know, and it is a great deal. I am sorry. I did warn you, and I will pray for you, which you will find cold comfort, and which is the only comfort I have left to give.

— Ilyen
does.subject: Reported

does.text:
A season without the guard in the streets, and I thank you. The chapel is quieter, as a house is when a fever breaks.

— Ilyen

opening.text: I have told the Interior minister what I heard. The rest is between you and your conscience, a room I will not enter.

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
The court has moved, and I will not choose a side in it with a Desk at my back; a shepherd does not choose between his sheep. I resign and return to the chapel, where no sides are taken, and I will hear whoever comes.

— Tomasz Ilyen

— Ilyen

opening.subject: Grace
opening.text:
You act gently on what the Desk brings you. That is grace in a ruler, and it is rarer than you know. The chapel will speak well of you, which in the long run matters more than the gazette, and the long run, as it happens, is my parish.

— Ilyen

does.text:
Understood. The chapel is open, and so is the safe; I never locked it, for there was nothing in it to be ashamed of. If you wish to talk, I am there most evenings, as are, you may like to know, a good many of your ministers.

— Ilyen

opening.text:
Your friend has the Desk, and I have gone back to the chapel, where the truest intelligence was always kept. If your friend is honest, I will hear nothing and tell you nothing. If not, I will hear it before anyone, and I will tell you, because a court is a parish and you are, for better or worse, one of my flock.

— Ilyen, lately of the Desk
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Jace
characters.bio: A belt smuggler turned informant turned director, because nobody else at court knew which rocks the pirates hid behind. No surname given, and nobody has asked twice. Holds a pardon she checks the wording of every month.

letters.appointed:
You gave a smuggler the Desk. Smart move, honestly; nobody else in this building knows the belt from a hole in the hull. Gonna be straight with you, 'cause I'm rubbish at the other thing. I know the pirates, I know the Syndicate's rocks, and I know who in your fleet's taking their coin. Keep my pardon in one piece and you get the lot. Let somebody tear it up and the belt gets me back, and the belt pays better than you, no offence.

— Jace, the Desk

loyal: Smuggler at the Desk, eh? Nobody else here knew the belt, so now you've got someone who does.
Belt's gone quiet. Quiet means somebody's loading, and I've got their schedule, so relax.
Nothing on the Desk today. Checked the rocks anyway, 'cause old habits and all that.
venal: Belt's quiet. Quiet costs a bit, mind, and the bit's going in my pocket.

loyal: Foreign hands inside, belt hands by the look of the knots. Give us a week and I'll hand you the whole crew with a bow on.
{target} had a crew in the fleet. Ran rocks with two of 'em back in the day, so let me have a chat before the suits get there.
Somebody got sounded out. Seen the sounder's face in a bar on a rock I'm not naming, but the name's in the file.
One of ours is sat in a {target} cell. Know the cell, know what the guard costs. You say go, I'm gone.
Sanctions on {target}, yeah? There'll be runners, and some of 'em are folks I owe. Bit awkward, that.
venal: Sanctions, lovely. I know every runner who'll break 'em, and half've already rung me.

loyal: It's tonight. Got a crew can hold the east gate; they're not the guard and they don't ask why, which is sort of the point.
Approved, sweet. Got a crew lined up already, and no, you don't want to know which.
Declined, fair enough. I'll still be watching the rocks, mind; can't switch it off.
No answer, huh. Out in the belt there's no such thing as unanswered, stuff just sort of happens.
Right then. Pardon's still good, yeah? Asking nice, the once.
I'm out. There's a berth in the belt with my name on it, always has been.
Morning, boss. Couple of skiffs shifted in the belt overnight, and I know whose they are.

does.text:
Right. Pardon's still good, yeah? Asking nice, once, and in writing. If it is, I go quiet and stay put in the capital. If it isn't, I'm off to the belt, and the belt's gonna want to know what I know. Rather not find out what I'd tell 'em.

— Jace

opening.text: Pirates hit us. Know whose skiffs, too, so let me work the belt my way, yeah?

Raiders hit a convoy, and I know the skiffs 'cause I crewed one. Let me run the belt my way: a marque here, a quiet word there, maybe a drink or two. Desk gets better at this when you let it, and I get a bit dirtier. Was dirty before, mind; pardon covers it.

— Jace
opening.subject: The belt, my way

does.text:
You let me work it, and the raids've stopped for a season. Pardon's starting to feel real. Cheers for that, and let's not make it weird, eh?

— Jace

You got back to the Desk before the Syndicate got back to me twice. Good timing, that. Clean again, mostly, and the mostly's only a little one.

— Jace

— Jace

does.text:
You reeled me in. Retainer's cancelled, and the crew's narked about it, but they're always narked. I'm yours, pardon and all.

— Jace

opening.text:
Your mate's got the Desk. Fine by me; kept the pardon, and that's all I ever wanted out of the chair. Still know the belt, though. If your mate needs the rocks explained, send 'em my way, and if your mate's from the belt, tell me now, 'cause I'd know the knots.

— Jace, lately of the Desk
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Gaius Vorne
characters.bio: A frontier magistrate who hanged a pirate governor and was promoted for it. Order first, always; believes a quiet street is a moral achievement and a crowd is a crime waiting for its moment. Reports honestly only to rulers he respects.

letters.appointed:
Prefect Vorne, Home Office, presenting. The undertaking is this: the provinces shall be kept quiet. Quiet is purchased with the guard, and the guard will be requested when the streets fill; upon approval the streets are cleared, upon refusal the streets are left to decide for themselves. A strong hand is reported to honestly. What is done under a weak one is not reported at all.

— G. Vorne, Prefect, Home Office

loyal: Order is the first duty of this Office, and every other duty exists to be served by it.
The provinces are quiet. That quiet was secured by the guard on two occasions and by a judge on one, and it is so entered in the record.
Muttering has been noted on three worlds and is tolerated within the law. Should it become a crowd, it will be treated as one.
cooling: The provinces are kept as quiet as a weak hand permits, and it is the duty of this Office to inform you that a weak hand permits very little.
brutus: The provinces are quiet. The reasons are no longer included in my reports, since it was not apparent that the reasons were wanted.

loyal: Approval is falling and crowds are forming. The guard is requested now, before they have formed in earnest, as the cost of order rises with every hour it is deferred.
Drift is recorded on the outer worlds. A judge is to be sent first and a garrison second; the judge is the cheaper instrument and, properly employed, the sufficient one.
brutus: Drift continues in the provinces. Which provinces is no longer reported by this Office; the chronicle will inform you in due course.

loyal: The cells have been broken and the streets restored to quiet. No apology is offered for either, and none is owed under the law.
brutus: The crackdown was effective. Command of the guard has since passed to this Office, as a matter of administrative efficiency.

loyal: Disorder is reported on {world}. The guard is to be sent first and bread after, for it has never been demonstrated to me that bread disperses a riot already in progress.
{world} has been lost. The guard was requested three times and three times refused; that fact will be recorded by the chronicle, and not by me.
The gazette is at our disposal for one week. A quiet gazette makes for a quiet street, and it is to be employed accordingly.
Troops are in motion without lawful order. The guard is held by this Office and is disposed toward order; you will state tonight which party the order is.
brutus: The matter is concluded. You will remain in your rooms, and the night will be made to pass without incident, as the guard prefers.

loyal: Approval is recorded. The streets will be cleared before midnight, by whatever measures the guard finds necessary.
The request is declined and so noted. The question is therefore left to the crowd, which will settle it in its own manner.
brutus: Declined, and so noted. Requests from this Office are hereby discontinued, and reports will be discontinued with them.

loyal: No answer was given within the time allowed. It is observed that a crowd does not wait upon an answer before it acts.
The dismissal is acknowledged. The guard rosters have been placed on your desk; the guard answers to the rosters, and it would be prudent that they be read.
brutus: The office is surrendered. It is known to the guard by whose hand the streets were kept quiet, and that knowledge is not surrendered with it.

loyal: This Office will not keep the streets for a hand unwilling to hold them. My resignation is submitted, effective immediately.
Report for the night: the streets remained empty throughout. That is the whole of the report, and the whole of the duty.

does.text:
Dismissal acknowledged. The guard rosters are on your desk; the guard answers to whoever reads them, and they were read by me for six years. It is advised that they be read. A weak hand that neglects them will find the streets have formed opinions.

— G. Vorne, Prefect

opening.subject: A strong hand
opening.text:
The guard was used, and quiet has been restored. Whose hand gave the order is known to the guard and to me. An honest report is owed to such a hand, and it will be rendered while the hand remains strong.

— G. Vorne, Prefect

does.text:
Dismissal acknowledged. The guard rosters are on your desk; the guard answers to whoever reads them, and they were read by me for six years. It is advised that they be read. A weak hand that neglects them will find the streets have formed opinions.

— G. Vorne, Prefect

opening.text: Requests for the guard have gone unanswered. Reports are henceforth limited to what a weak hand can be expected to bear.

does.text:
Four requests have been submitted and four met with silence. The office will be retained and the streets kept as quiet as a weak hand permits. Honest reporting on the provinces is, however, discontinued as of this date: the truth was declined when it was cheap, and it is no longer cheap. Notice of the next secession will be found in the chronicle.

— G. Vorne, Prefect
does.subject: What a weak hand can bear

does.text:
Dismissal acknowledged. The guard rosters are on your desk; the guard answers to whoever reads them, and they were read by me for six years. It is advised that they be read. A weak hand that neglects them will find the streets have formed opinions.

— G. Vorne, Prefect

opening.text: The provinces are quiet. The reasons are no longer reported.

does.text:
The guard has been used. Honest reporting is resumed, and it will not be resumed a second time.

— G. Vorne
does.subject: Honest again

does.text:
Dismissal acknowledged. The guard rosters are on your desk; the guard answers to whoever reads them, and they were read by me for six years. It is advised that they be read. A weak hand that neglects them will find the streets have formed opinions.

— G. Vorne, Prefect

— G. Vorne, Prefect

opening.text:
Your friend has been given the Home Office. The guard is not acquainted with your friend and answers to me until instructed otherwise; no such instruction has been issued. I remain at court. Order is not removed when the chair changes hands, only held in abeyance.

— G. Vorne, lately of the Home Office
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Henrike Ostrova
characters.bio: Governed the richest world in the empire for twenty years before the founding, and believes the capital is a guest in her provinces. Took the Home Office to keep it from a centraliser. Her home world would follow her out of the empire, and she knows it.

letters.appointed:
I accepted the Home Office chiefly to keep it out of the hands of someone who imagines the capital rules the provinces, which it does not, my dear; it is a guest in them, and guests who forget their manners are, in my experience, shown the door. I shall propose that the provinces govern themselves while the capital collects what it is owed. Build the administration out there, among the worlds, and you will have my loyalty, which is not a small thing to have; build it here, and you will discover what my home world thinks of guests.

— Henrike Ostrova, Home Office

loyal: The capital, as I have had occasion to remind several governments before yours, is a guest in the provinces, and I have come principally to see that it remembers its manners.
The provinces have run themselves this month, as provinces will when nobody in the capital interferes, and the capital has collected what it is owed, which is all it was ever meant to do.
cooling: The capital has taken to issuing instructions to the governors again, and the governors, who have known me for twenty years and the capital for rather less, have been forwarding them to me.
brutus: The provinces look to their own, as they always have, and my own world, which I governed for twenty years before anyone here had heard of it, looks to me.

loyal: The outer worlds drift because they are governed from a desk a month away by people who have never seen them; let them govern themselves and the drifting stops, there being nothing left to drift from.
brutus: The provinces are drifting from the capital, I grant you, though I cannot help noticing that none of them is drifting from me.

loyal: Approval falls in the capital, where I gather it often does, while in the provinces it holds, for the simple reason that I visit them and you, my dear, do not.
{world} has gone, as worlds governed from a desk generally do, and I did say so, at some length, to anyone in the capital who cared to listen.
brutus: {world} has gone, and the other worlds are watching to see what the capital does about it, as, I think I ought to tell you, is my own.

loyal: A crackdown, then. The provinces always notice when the capital sends soldiers where it ought to have sent judges, and they will remember it long after the capital has forgotten it happened.

We have more worlds than offices, and the offices, if they are to be built at all, belong on the worlds rather than in the capital; I have said so politely, and I do not intend to say it politely again.
Troops are moving, though my home world's levies, you will be relieved to hear, are not moving yet; tell me tonight whose side the capital is on, and I shall tell you where the levies stand.
Approved, I see. The governors will hear of it from me, which is how they have preferred to hear things for twenty years.
Declined, I see. The governors will hear of that from me as well, and I shall try to make it sound less foolish than it is.
brutus: Declined, then. My home world will hear of it from me, and I should not count on my softening it for them.

loyal: No answer, once again. The provinces have grown quite accustomed to the capital not answering, which is, when one thinks about it, precisely why they have me.
Take the office, by all means. The governors know my address perfectly well, several of them having been my guests there over the years.
brutus: Take the office, if you must, though you will find that my home world has opinions on the matter and is not at all shy about expressing them.

loyal: I am resigning, and I am going home, to the one world in this empire where I have never once been made to feel like a guest.
Good morning. The provinces slept soundly, as provinces do when left alone, whereas the capital, I am told, did not sleep at all.

does.text:
Take the office, by all means. The governors know my address, several of them having stayed there. I am going home, where I have never been a guest, and where people will ask me what the capital is actually for; I shall think very carefully about what to tell them.

— H. Ostrova

opening.subject: Guests
opening.text: Twice now the Home Office has asked the capital to let the provinces govern themselves, and twice the capital has failed to answer, which is, of course, an answer of a kind. I shall therefore put it plainly, my dear: the civil reforms, adopted as policy, with offices on the worlds, governors the worlds have chosen, and the capital collecting what it is owed and not a great deal more. Sign it, and I am yours for life; refuse it, and my home world will ask me what the capital is for.

does.text:
The capital has answered four times by not answering, a habit I had thought confined to junior clerks. My home world has asked me what the capital is for, and for the first time in twenty years I had no answer to give.

— H. Ostrova
does.subject: What the capital is for

does.text:
Take the office, by all means. The governors know my address, several of them having stayed there. I am going home, where I have never been a guest, and where people will ask me what the capital is actually for; I shall think very carefully about what to tell them.

— H. Ostrova

opening.text: My home world asks what the capital is for, and I have ceased troubling to reply.

does.text:
You have answered at last. My home world will wait, being rather good at it; it waited twenty years for me.

— H. Ostrova
does.subject: Waiting

does.text:
Another season, and my home world has decided what the capital is for: not very much, I am sorry to say. I intend to help it act accordingly. I should have preferred loyalty, but you have priced it beyond my means.

— H. Ostrova
does.subject: Decided

does.text:
Take the office, by all means. The governors know my address, several of them having stayed there. I am going home, where I have never been a guest, and where people will ask me what the capital is actually for; I shall think very carefully about what to tell them.

— H. Ostrova

You have begun, at last, to listen, so I have told my home world to wait, which it will do for now, as shall I.

— H. Ostrova
does.subject: For now

opening.subject: For life
opening.text:
You built it on the worlds, as I asked, and so the governors are yours now, as am I; I said I would be and I meant it, for a guest who remembers that he is a guest becomes, in time, a friend. My home world sends its regards, which it does not send often, and never lightly.

— H. Ostrova

does.text:
Take the office, by all means. The governors know my address, several of them having stayed there. I am going home, where I have never been a guest, and where people will ask me what the capital is actually for; I shall think very carefully about what to tell them.

— H. Ostrova

opening.text:
Your friend has been given the Home Office, and the governors have been forwarding me your friend's letters, since they have never heard of your friend and have known me for twenty years. I remain at court, though I should far rather be at home. Should your friend take it into their head to centralise, I shall hear of it from twelve worlds well before you hear of it from one.

— H. Ostrova, lately of the Home Office
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Ade Lumumba-Tarn
characters.bio: A frontier preacher who became a governor who became a minister by being the only person the outposts trust. Still sleeps in a dome when he visits. Believes the frontier is the empire's conscience and that the capital forgets this roughly once a season.

letters.appointed:
Citizen Lumumba-Tarn, Home Office. Why Citizen? Because the frontier gave me that name, and the frontier is why I am here. I will speak for the outposts in every brief: the strikes, the fevers, the folk who ask to go home. I ask one thing, and I ask it plain. Do not build camps. Do not build them. The frontier is where people go to be free, and the day the capital makes it a prison is the day I carry the frontier out of the capital's reach. That is a promise and not a plot, and it only becomes a plot if you make it one.

— Ade Lumumba-Tarn, for the frontier

loyal: The frontier sent me here, and the frontier will hear from me, and I will keep sending word back to it for as long as I sit in this chair.
The outposts are holding. There is fever on one and a strike on another, and I have written to both, and I wrote to every soul by name.
The frontier is quiet. And what is quiet out there? Quiet is nobody dying this week, and I count that as a blessing every time it comes.
cooling: The outposts write to me, and I write back. Who writes to the outposts from the capital? Nobody does, and the outposts have noticed, and so have I.
brutus: The frontier looks to me now. Does the capital look to the frontier? It does not look at all, not once, not this whole long season.

loyal: The outer worlds are drifting, and the cure is a visit, a plain visit in the dust. I will go with you, because they know my boots and they know my face.
Approval falls in the capital, but out on the frontier it holds. Why does it hold? It holds because somebody answers the letters, and that somebody is me.
The crews have struck, and they should be paid, and the one who carries the pay should be someone who has worked a shift in the dust. I have worked that shift, and I will carry it.
There is a riot on {world}, and what does a riot want? Bread, first and last. On the frontier the bread is most of the riot, and sometimes it is all of it.
The guard is on frontier streets. I was a frontier street once, a boy in the dust under a dome, and I will not forget this, and they will not forget it either.
cooling: A crackdown, and I warned you of it, and I warned you plainly, and here it is all the same.

loyal: {world} has gone. It was a frontier world, and who from the capital had been there this year? Nobody had. I had been, and I slept in its domes.
Troops are moving. The frontier levies answer to me, and they are far off in the dust; tell me whether I should call them in, and tell me for whom.
Approved, and thank you. The outposts will hear of it tonight, every one of them, and every one of them by name.
Declined. I will tell the outposts the capital is busy, and they will nod, because they have heard the capital is busy before, many times before.
No answer came. The frontier knows that silence well; silence is how the capital has always spoken to it.
So be it. The outpost letters are on your desk, and they want answers; I answered every one, and now that work is yours to carry.
brutus: Take the office. And when it is all said and done, the frontier will remember who answered its letters, and it was not the capital.

loyal: I resign. The frontier needs a voice more than the capital needs a minister, and so I am going back to the dust, where a voice is still heard.
Morning. Three outposts wrote in the night, and I have answered two of them. The third has a fever, and a fever needs more than a letter, so I am going there today.

does.text:
So be it. The outpost letters are on your desk, by name and by world. I answered them. Will you? The outposts will know the difference. I am going back to the frontier, and hear me once more: build no camps while I am gone, for the dust carries word, and I will hear.

— Ade Lumumba-Tarn

opening.text: The guard on frontier streets. I was a frontier street once, and I will not forget it, not ever.

You sent the guard against people who went to the frontier to be free of exactly that. I will stay in the chair, and I will keep answering the letters, but I have written to the outposts and told them the truth, the plain truth: the capital forgot them this season. Do it a second time and I will carry the frontier out of your reach. That was a promise when I made it, and it is a promise still, and only you can turn it into a plot.

— Ade Lumumba-Tarn
opening.subject: A promise

does.text:
A second time. The frontier heard, and the frontier asked me to lead it, and I said yes. So here it is, the plot you made out of a promise. I am sorry for it; I would far rather have stayed your minister.

— Ade Lumumba-Tarn
does.subject: The plot you made

does.text:
After the guard, you listened, and you listened again. The outposts noticed, and I noticed. So the promise stands, and the plot, the plot does not exist.

— Ade Lumumba-Tarn
does.subject: Noticed

does.text:
So be it. The outpost letters are on your desk, by name and by world. I answered them. Will you? The outposts will know the difference. I am going back to the frontier, and hear me once more: build no camps while I am gone, for the dust carries word, and I will hear.

— Ade Lumumba-Tarn

You have begun to answer the frontier, so I told it to wait. Will it wait? It will wait for me, a while.

— Ade Lumumba-Tarn
does.subject: A while

opening.subject: Heard
opening.text:
You answer the frontier's letters. Not once in my whole life did anyone from the capital do that, not once, and now you do. The outposts will stay, and I will stay with them, as long as the letters keep being answered.

— Ade Lumumba-Tarn

does.text:
So be it. The outpost letters are on your desk, by name and by world. I answered them. Will you? The outposts will know the difference. I am going back to the frontier, and hear me once more: build no camps while I am gone, for the dust carries word, and I will hear.

— Ade Lumumba-Tarn

opening.text:
Your friend has the Home Office, but the outposts do not know your friend, so they keep writing to me. And I keep answering, because somebody must, and I will tell you what they say. If your friend builds a camp I will tell you that too, one time only, and after that the frontier will tell you in its own voice.

— Ade Lumumba-Tarn, lately of the Home Office
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Anselm Vey
characters.bio: A name older than the state and a wine cellar older than the name. Has dined with every court in the galaxy and remembers what they served. Believes war is a failure of lunch and that an old family's word is the only treaty worth signing.

letters.appointed:
Charmed, truly, and rather touched. I have dined at every court that matters and at several that, between ourselves, do not, and I shall keep them sweet, which is all diplomacy has ever been: keeping people sweet, course after course, until they quite forget to be dangerous. I accept gifts from ambassadors, as everyone does; one simply does not refuse a man who has brought a good vintage. I shall propose peace, always, as my father did. And should you make some vulgar war upon an old family, I shall be very distressed, and old families, when distressed, write to one another.

— A. Vey, Foreign Office, from the cellar

loyal: Charmed, truly. The embassies will want refurbishing, of course, as they always do after a change of government, and as it happens the contractors are old friends.
The courts are sweet this month, and one of them sent round a case of something I had not tasted since my father was alive, which you may think a small thing, but these things, my dear, matter.
Two courts send their regards, and I sent rather better ones back, because it is, you understand, and has been since my grandfather's day, a competition.
cooling: I go on keeping five courts warm, without instructions, over a great many dinners, and between the fish and the meat they have begun to wonder aloud whether there is a government behind me.
venal: Relations are cordial, cordial as a well-kept port, and cordiality, as anyone at an old table knows, is kept up by gifts, which run both ways, and some of which are rather good.

loyal: I should accept, and with grace, since their terms are a good deal better than their position and, I might add, they served a very good lunch.
venal: Oh, accept, I think; their ambassador has been most attentive, these past weeks, to my cellar.

loyal: Not yet, I think; let it breathe a week, like any decent red, for a week turns most offers into better ones or into nothing at all.
Peace, if you please; war is, when one considers it over a decent claret, merely a failure of lunch, and so I propose to arrange a lunch.
{target} is tired, poor things; I know their foreign minister rather well, we were at school together and he has not changed a bit, so give me a room and a long table.
War on {target}? On an old family, whose cellar my grandfather once admired? No, I think not; I shall propose peace instead, as I always do.
Signed, over a rather good vintage, and {target} will in due course betray us politely, which is, after all, the only civilised way.
We have broken our word to an old family, which one simply does not do, and so I shall spend a year at their table making amends, course by course, and I would be grateful if you did not help.
cooling: We have broken a treaty I once raised a glass to, on a lovely evening, and abroad I shall go on smiling about it, though here, I find, I shall not.

loyal: {target} sends an ultimatum, which is terribly vulgar, the sort of thing new money does; stall them a week and I shall have their ambassador to dinner.
The rebels have sent a gift along with their request, very thoughtful, and I have left it unopened, because one does not, you see, until one has decided.
Approved, and splendid; I shall have it mentioned in all the right rooms by dinner.
Declined, and quite right; I shall tell the courts we are considering, and one can consider, I assure you, for years, as I have.
It went unanswered, and so the ambassador's gift went unthanked, which simply would not do, and so I thanked them myself, as one must.
Of course, of course. The courts will ask, naturally, and I shall say I am resting, which they will not believe, and that, in its way, is also useful.
brutus: You may have the office, by all means, draughts and all; the ambassadors have my private address, and most of them, I find, have used it.

loyal: I resign, then, courteously, as my family always has, and in writing to three courts, who will, I rather think, be sorry.
Good morning. Two courts send regards, and one sends a warning baked in the shape of regards, like a pie with a blade in it; I have dined there often enough to know the shape.

does.text:
Of course, of course. The courts will ask where I have gone, and I shall say I am resting, which none will believe, and which is, in its quiet way, rather useful. The ambassadors have my address, on the backs of a great many menus, and I should not be surprised if they went on using it.

— Vey

Of course, of course. The courts will ask where I have gone, and I shall say I am resting, which none will believe, and which is, in its quiet way, rather useful. The ambassadors have my address, on the backs of a great many menus, and I should not be surprised if they went on using it.

— Vey

opening.subject: Sweet
opening.text:
You take the Foreign Office's advice, and so the courts are sweet; nobody has sent so much as a warning in a season, which at my age is better than a fortnight on the coast. I shall stay as long as there are lunches, and there are, I am pleased to say, always lunches.

— Vey

does.text:
Of course, of course. The courts will ask where I have gone, and I shall say I am resting, which none will believe, and which is, in its quiet way, rather useful. The ambassadors have my address, on the backs of a great many menus, and I should not be surprised if they went on using it.

— Vey

opening.text: A war, and upon an old family, of all people; I am very distressed, and old families, when distressed, write to one another.

You have made war, and I did warn you, over that very pleasant supper, that I should be distressed, and I am. Old families write to one another at such times; it is how we have outlasted every government, and shall outlast yours. I have written, at some length, saying nothing whatever about the fleet and a very great deal about you.

— Vey
opening.subject: Distressed

does.text:
Peace, then; I shall arrange the lunch, a good white to begin. We shall not speak of the letters; old families never do.

— Vey
does.subject: Lunch

does.text:
Of course, of course. The courts will ask where I have gone, and I shall say I am resting, which none will believe, and which is, in its quiet way, rather useful. The ambassadors have my address, on the backs of a great many menus, and I should not be surprised if they went on using it.

— Vey

Peace, at last, and the letters may stop; they were only ever about you, my dear, and now you have been reasonable. Lunch, I think, is on Thursday.

— Vey
does.subject: Thursday

does.text:
Of course, of course. The courts will ask where I have gone, and I shall say I am resting, which none will believe, and which is, in its quiet way, rather useful. The ambassadors have my address, on the backs of a great many menus, and I should not be surprised if they went on using it.

— Vey

opening.text:
Your friend has the Foreign Office. How exciting for the courts, who do so love a new face at table, briefly, the way one loves a new cook until the second week. I remain at court and at dinner, which at my age are the same thing. And if your friend is rude to an old family, I shall hear of it, I promise you, before the soup.

— Vey, lately of the Foreign Office
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Tariq Sol-Benedek
characters.bio: Negotiated the Banking Clan's first loan to a frontier world and got the world a better rate than the Clan intended. Thinks every treaty is a trade route in disguise and every sanction a tariff with a flag on it. Quick, warm, and allergic to closed borders.

letters.appointed:
Thank you! Here's what the Foreign Office is for, in my hands: trade. A treaty is a trade route with a seal on it. An alliance is a shared tariff. A war is a closed border, plus casualties. I'll bring you company charters, host policy and open lanes, and I'll oppose every sanction you ever float, because a sanction is a tariff we pay ourselves. Keep the borders open and I'll keep the courts friendly; on my ledger that's one line, not two.

— T. Sol-Benedek, Foreign Office (lanes open, always)

loyal: A treaty is a trade route with a seal on it, and I plan to seal several by spring!
Lanes open, courts friendly. On my ledger that's one line, not two!
Two courts want to trade, one wants to talk. Guess where I'm spending my afternoon.
cooling: The borders are closing one tariff at a time, and I've logged an objection against every single one.
brutus: The courts still talk to me about trade. With this government they've stopped talking about anything at all.

loyal: Accept! Read past the pride and there's a lane in it, a good one, with margin.
Refuse it, warmly. Their offer closes a lane, and a closed lane is the one item I won't sign for.
Sanctions on {target}? That's a tariff we pay ourselves with a flag stuck on it. My objection's in writing, and meanwhile I'll keep the lane open by other routes.
cooling: Sanctions again! I objected the first time, and this time I'm objecting louder.

loyal: {target} has sanctioned us. Fine! A sanction is just a bargaining position in uniform, and I'll have that lane reopened inside two months.
Signed! Three trade routes in the fine print that nobody spotted but me, and they'll spot them soon enough.
Envoy's off to {target} with samples, not gifts. Gifts are for old families; samples close deals.
Peace with {target}, please. The war's shut four lanes, and once they reopen the peace pays for itself inside a season.
A new state! Recognise it fast, because new states need trade partners and they always remember who signed first.
Approved! The lane opens with the next convoy.
Declined, so the lane stays shut, and somebody else will open it and pocket the margin.
No answer. Trade doesn't wait for one, it reroutes, and it's rerouting now.
Understood! The lane maps are on your desk, every closed lane tagged with who closed it.
I resign. A court with open borders has asked me over, and frankly I'd rather trade than sulk.
Morning! Three convoys cleared overnight, one court sent a tariff, and I've already answered the tariff.

does.text:
Understood, no hard feelings. The lane maps are on your desk, every closed lane tagged with who closed it and when. A court with open borders has asked me over, and I think I'll go; better to trade for somebody than sulk at home. And nothing I know about your lanes is secret. It's all on the maps!

— Sol-Benedek

opening.subject: Lanes
opening.text: Twice now the Foreign Office has asked for open lanes, and twice the court hasn't answered. So here's the deal: open trade as a policy, one signature, done. Every court I deal with asks about lanes before anything else. You give me the lanes, I deliver the courts!

does.text:
Four silences, and counting. The lanes close one tariff at a time, I file an objection for every one, and the court doesn't read them. I'm still at my desk. But I'm reading the letters from that open-border court a lot more carefully than I was.

— Sol-Benedek
does.subject: More carefully

does.text:
Understood, no hard feelings. The lane maps are on your desk, every closed lane tagged with who closed it and when. A court with open borders has asked me over, and I think I'll go; better to trade for somebody than sulk at home. And nothing I know about your lanes is secret. It's all on the maps!

— Sol-Benedek

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
A season of closed lanes and unread objections, and the ledger doesn't balance. I resign the Foreign Office. A court with open borders has asked me over, and I'd rather trade for them than sulk for you. The lane maps are on your desk.

— Tariq Sol-Benedek

Understood, no hard feelings. The lane maps are on your desk, every closed lane tagged with who closed it and when. A court with open borders has asked me over, and I think I'll go; better to trade for somebody than sulk at home. And nothing I know about your lanes is secret. It's all on the maps!

— Sol-Benedek

opening.subject: Open
opening.text:
Lanes open, courts friendly, just like I said: one line on the ledger! I'll stay as long as the borders do. And thanks for reading the maps; most rulers don't.

— Sol-Benedek

does.text:
Understood, no hard feelings. The lane maps are on your desk, every closed lane tagged with who closed it and when. A court with open borders has asked me over, and I think I'll go; better to trade for somebody than sulk at home. And nothing I know about your lanes is secret. It's all on the maps!

— Sol-Benedek

opening.text:
Your friend has the Foreign Office. Hope they like trade, because the courts will ask about that first and their politics second. I'm still at court, though an open-border court has written to me and I haven't said no yet. Keep the lanes open and I won't say yes!

— Sol-Benedek, lately of the Foreign Office
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Maren Oduya
characters.bio: A missionary in a rival court for ten years; came home fluent in their language, their liturgy and their lies. Unforgiving in the precise way of someone who has forgiven professionally. Believes the faith's enemies should be isolated, and knows which court they are.

letters.appointed:
Sister Oduya, to the Foreign Office. Ten years I dwelt in the court I will not name in writing, and I came home knowing what they are. Let there be sanctions upon them, and friendship with all the rest. Any peace you make I will serve, save one. If you sign a treaty with that court, I will carry it to the Interior minister and name it for what it is: heresy at the top. I tell you this now, and kindly, so that it shall never come to you as a surprise.

— M. Oduya, Foreign Office, in faith

loyal: Ten years I dwelt in their court and learned their liturgy and their lies; and the lies, I found, rhyme.
The courts are warm, all save one, and that one I keep cold. This is the whole of the policy, and it is sufficient.
Three courts send regards, and one sends scripture. The scripture was in error, and I have corrected it.
cooling: I keep the courts warm, though no instruction comes. One I keep cold on my own authority, and no voice has yet been raised against it.
brutus: The courts ask who speaks for this empire, and I answer them: the faithful. I am the faithful.

loyal: Accept. They are not the court I mean, and their terms are honest; honest terms are not to be refused.
Refuse it. I know the hand that drafted this, for I taught that hand to draft, and the snare lies in the second clause.
Sanctions upon {target}. That is good; and if it be the court I mean, it is better.
A treaty with {target}. If it is the court I mean, the Interior minister already has my judgement of it. If it is not, then peace be upon it, and my congratulations.
{target} has broken its word. This was foretold; I foretold it, in the first letter I ever wrote you.
{target} accuses us of spying. Ten years I lived among them, and of course we were. Answer them with scripture, for against scripture they have no answer.
Peace with {target}, unless {target} is the court I mean. Then let it be patience, for patience is peace that keeps its eyes open.
A new state asks to be recognised. If it has broken from the court I mean, recognise it before the noon bell.
Approved. By evening it shall be spoken in the right chapels.
Declined. I will pray upon it, and my prayers are not long.
No answer was given. In a ruler, silence is a kind of heresy; a small one, but it is written down.
